fuentes/capitulacion-de-toledo-1529/auto.texto: Crown of Castile (signed by Empress Isabel on behalf of Charles V)

fuentes/capitulacion-de-toledo-1529/sopo.texto: Royal capitulación signed in Toledo on July 26, 1529

fuentes/capitulacion-de-toledo-1529/resu.texto: Contract between the Crown, represented by Empress Isabel in the absence of Charles V, and Francisco Pizarro for the conquest of Peru. It gave Pizarro the titles of governor, captain general, adelantado, and alguacil mayor of New Castile, for some two hundred leagues of coast south of Tempula (Santiago), with his salary to be paid from the revenues of the land. Almagro received only the stewardship of the fortress of Tumbes and hidalgo status, and Luque the bishopric of Tumbes and the title of protector of the Indians. It included the usual clauses on the royal fifth, the good treatment of the Indians, and the presence of clergy, and it allowed him to bring enslaved Africans.

fuentes/capitulacion-de-toledo-1529/por_.texto: It is the legal basis of the conquest of Peru and the origin of Almagro’s resentment, which ended in war between the two partners. It shows that the conquest was a private enterprise authorized and regulated by the Crown.

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/titulo.texto: True Account of the Conquest of Peru and the Province of Cuzco Called New Castile

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/soporte.texto: Book printed in Seville in July 1534

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/resumen.texto: Chronicle by Pizarro’s secretary, written at his commission and published in Seville in 1534. It narrates the voyages from Panama, the march to Cajamarca, the capture of Atahualpa on November 16, 1532, and the assembling of the ransom, with figures for the booty, and it includes Miguel de Estete’s account of Hernando Pizarro’s journey to Pachacamac and Jauja. It justifies the conquest and Pizarro’s conduct: it presents the attack on Cajamarca as a response to Atahualpa’s contempt for the book offered to him by the friar Valverde, and it estimates some two thousand Indigenous people killed that day.

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/por_que.texto: It is the official account of the conquest, written by a witness who was also an interested party. Together with Mena, Sancho, and Hernando Pizarro’s letter, it forms the core of the direct testimony on Cajamarca.

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/leer.0..texto: Seville edition of 1891, with Miguel de Estete’s account, on Internet Archive

fuentes/verdadera-relacion-xerez/leer.1..texto: English translation by Clements Markham in Reports on the Discovery of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1872), on Internet Archive

fuentes/la-conquista-del-peru-mena/titul.texto: The Conquest of Peru, Called New Castile

fuentes/la-conquista-del-peru-mena/sopor.texto: Pamphlet printed in Seville in April 1534, without an author’s name (the “Sevillian Anonymous”)

fuentes/la-conquista-del-peru-mena/resum.texto: Brief account of Pizarro’s expedition from 1531 to the division of the ransom, published unsigned in Seville in April 1534 and attributed to Cristóbal de Mena by Raúl Porras Barrenechea. It is less favorable to Pizarro than Xerez’s account: it describes more bluntly the violence of the march and of Cajamarca and the greed for gold, and its author complains about the division of the booty.

fuentes/la-conquista-del-peru-mena/por_q.texto: It was the first printed chronicle of the conquest of Peru, and it shows that different versions of events circulated among the conquistadors themselves.

fuentes/carta-de-hernando-pizarro-1533/t.texto: Letter from Hernando Pizarro to the Judges of the Audiencia of Santo Domingo

fuentes/carta-de-hernando-pizarro-1533/s.texto: Letter dated in Panama in November 1533, preserved by Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo in his Historia general y natural de las Indias

fuentes/carta-de-hernando-pizarro-1533/r.texto: Account that Hernando Pizarro wrote while passing through Panama, on his way to Spain with the royal fifth, about the capture of Atahualpa and about his own journey from Cajamarca to Pachacamac and Jauja in search of gold in early 1533. It describes the plundering of the sanctuary of Pachacamac, the Inca road with its bridges, storehouses, and tambos, and the capture of the general Chalcuchímac.

fuentes/carta-de-hernando-pizarro-1533/p.texto: It is the earliest testimony by one of the leaders of the conquest and a firsthand document on the Qhapaq Ñan and the coastal sanctuaries at the time of contact.

fuentes/carta-de-hernando-pizarro-1533/l.texto: English translation by Clements Markham in Reports on the Discovery of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1872), on Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-sancho/titulo.texto: Account of the Conquest of Peru

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-sancho/soporte.texto: Account signed by Pizarro and his officers in July 1534; the original was lost and is known through the Italian translation by Giovanni Battista Ramusio (1556)

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-sancho/resumen.texto: Continuation of Xerez’s chronicle written by Pedro Sancho de la Hoz, who succeeded him as Pizarro’s secretary. It covers events from the execution of Atahualpa to mid-1534: the march to Cusco, the battles with Atahualpa’s generals, the burning of Chalcuchímac, the investiture of Manco Inca, and the Spanish founding of Cusco, with one of the first descriptions of the city and of the fortress of Sacsayhuamán.

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-sancho/por_que.texto: It is the most detailed direct testimony on Inca Cusco at the time of the Spanish occupation, written as an official report for the king.

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-pizarro/titulo.texto: Account of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-pizarro/soport.texto: Manuscript completed in Arequipa in 1571; first published in 1844

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-pizarro/resume.texto: Memoirs of a cousin of Francisco Pizarro who served as a page and soldier during the capture of Atahualpa, the siege of Cusco, and the civil wars. It gives firsthand details about Atahualpa in captivity, the cult of the Inca mummies, the Pizarro brothers’ treatment of Manco Inca, and the cruelty of both sides in the civil wars. Written almost forty years after the events, it defends his family and the conquistadors against the criticisms of Las Casas’s followers.

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-pizarro/por_qu.texto: It is one of the richest accounts by a witness to the conquest, with information on Inca society that does not appear in other chronicles.

fuentes/relacion-de-pedro-pizarro/leer.0.texto: English translation by Philip Ainsworth Means (Hakluyt Society, 1921), volume 1, on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-del-peru-zarate/titulo.texto: History of the Discovery and Conquest of Peru

fuentes/historia-del-peru-zarate/soporte.texto: Book printed in Antwerp by Martín Nucio (1555)

fuentes/historia-del-peru-zarate/resumen.texto: History written by an official of the Royal Treasury who arrived in Peru in 1544. It summarizes the conquest on the basis of testimony and recounts in detail, as a witness, Gonzalo Pizarro’s rebellion against the New Laws until his defeat by La Gasca. It includes a book on the geography and customs of the Indians. It was widely read in Europe and was soon translated into Italian and English.

fuentes/historia-del-peru-zarate/por_que.texto: For decades it was the standard printed history of Peru. Its author served the Crown and, under compulsion, the rebels, and he wrote carefully so as not to commit himself.

fuentes/historia-del-peru-zarate/leer.0..texto: Sixteenth-century Seville edition, on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-del-peru-diego-fernande.texto: First and Second Parts of the History of Peru

History of the civil wars of Peru written at the commission of Viceroy Andrés Hurtado de Mendoza. The first part recounts the rebellion of Francisco Hernández Girón (1553-1554), and the second that of Gonzalo Pizarro and the government of La Gasca, with the negotiations with Sayri Túpac. Its author, a soldier on the royalist side, used official documents and testimony. The Council of the Indies ordered the book collected shortly after it was published.
It is the main source on Hernández Girón’s rebellion and an example of how the Crown controlled what was published about Peru.
First part, Lima edition of 1913, on Internet Archive

fuentes/probanzas-de-los-huancas/titulo.texto: Service Records of the Huanca Curacas

fuentes/probanzas-de-los-huancas/autor.texto: Huanca curacas of the Jauja valley (Don Felipe Guacrapáucar and others)

fuentes/probanzas-de-los-huancas/soporte.texto: Service records presented before the Audiencia of Lima (1558, 1560, and 1561); published by Waldemar Espinoza Soriano in 1971

fuentes/probanzas-de-los-huancas/resumen.texto: Case files in which the lords of the three Huanca repartimientos of the Mantaro valley, among them Don Felipe Guacrapáucar, petitioned the king for favors for having helped the Spanish from 1533 onward against Atahualpa’s armies, against Manco Inca, and in the civil wars. They include lists of the men, women, llamas, maize, clothing, and other goods they handed over to the Spanish, read by the curacas from their quipus before the notary.

fuentes/probanzas-de-los-huancas/por_que.texto: Written to obtain favors, they may enlarge the services performed, but their detailed accounts show that the conquest was also a war of Andean peoples against the Incas, and the cost of that alliance for the allies themselves. They are also one of the best examples of quipus transcribed into writing.

fuentes/instruccion-de-titu-cusi/titulo.texto: Instruction of the Inca Don Diego de Castro Titu Cusi Yupanqui to the Licentiate Lope García de Castro

fuentes/instruccion-de-titu-cusi/soporte.texto: Account dictated in Quechua in Vilcabamba, rendered into Spanish by the Augustinian friar Marcos García and written down by the mestizo Martín de Pando (1570); published in 1916

fuentes/instruccion-de-titu-cusi/resumen.texto: Account dictated by the Inca of Vilcabamba so that former governor García de Castro could present it to the king. It tells the conquest from Manco Inca’s side: the arrival of the Spanish, the capture of Atahualpa, the humiliations and imprisonment of Manco by the Pizarros to extract gold from him, his uprising, and his death at the hands of the Spaniards he had sheltered in Vitcos. It asks the king to recognize his rights and grant favors to him and his son.

fuentes/instruccion-de-titu-cusi/por_que.texto: It is the most direct Inca version of the conquest, though it is also a political argument: Titu Cusi was negotiating with the Crown and presents his father as a legitimate lord who was betrayed.

fuentes/instruccion-de-titu-cusi/leer.0..texto: Digital edition by the Fundación Ignacio Larramendi (2020), under the title Relación de la conquista del Perú y hechos del inca Manco II, on Internet Archive

fuentes/tratado-de-las-doce-dudas/soport.texto: Manuscript treatise addressed to Philip II (1564)

fuentes/tratado-de-las-doce-dudas/resume.texto: Las Casas’s response to twelve questions of conscience raised from Peru about the conquest and the encomiendas of that kingdom. He argues that the conquest of Peru was unjust, that the goods taken from Atahualpa and the Incas had to be returned, that the encomenderos were obliged to return what they had collected, and that the king should return government to the heirs of the Incas, reserving only a higher sovereignty for himself. It was Las Casas’s last major work.

fuentes/tratado-de-las-doce-dudas/por_qu.texto: It is the most radical formulation of Las Casas’s critique applied to Peru, and the text against which the Parecer de Yucay and Viceroy Toledo’s policy reacted.

fuentes/parecer-de-yucay/soporte.texto: Anonymous letter-treatise dated in the Yucay valley on March 16, 1571

fuentes/parecer-de-yucay/resumen.texto: Anonymous text, which most scholars attribute to the Dominican García de Toledo, cousin of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, written during the viceroy’s general inspection. To refute Las Casas, it argues that the Incas were recent tyrants who had usurped lordship from the curacas, that for this reason the king of Spain was the legitimate lord of Peru, and that the wealth of the mines was like a dowry that God had given those lands to attract preachers. It criticizes religious men who questioned the Spanish titles.

fuentes/parecer-de-yucay/por_que_importa.texto: It is a key piece of Viceroy Toledo’s campaign to deny the legitimacy of the Incas, together with the Informaciones and Sarmiento de Gamboa’s History. It shows that the “Inca tyranny” was a political argument of the time, not a neutral conclusion.

fuentes/ordenanzas-del-virrey-toledo/tit.texto: Ordinances of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo

fuentes/ordenanzas-del-virrey-toledo/sop.texto: Ordinances, provisions, and instructions issued during his government; edited by Guillermo Lohmann Villena and María Justina Sarabia Viejo as Disposiciones gubernativas para el virreinato del Perú (1986-1989)

fuentes/ordenanzas-del-virrey-toledo/res.texto: Set of rules that the viceroy issued during his general inspection and his government to reorganize Peru: the resettlement of Indians into towns with a Spanish layout and Indigenous cabildos, the tribute assessment, the mita for the mines of Potosí and Huancavelica, the duties of corregidores, curacas, and doctrinal priests, mining, and the regime of the cities. It includes protective provisions, such as wages, limits on working days, and limits on the services that curacas and priests could demand, alongside the burdens of the new order.

fuentes/ordenanzas-del-virrey-toledo/por.texto: They were the basis of colonial administration in the Andes for two centuries. Indigenous authors such as Guaman Poma and the caciques of the Memorial de Charcas criticized their effects on the peoples.

fuentes/memorial-de-charcas/soporte.texto: Memorial addressed to the king from the Audiencia of La Plata; published by Waldemar Espinoza Soriano in 1969

fuentes/memorial-de-charcas/resumen.texto: Petition from the lords of the Charcas, Caracara, Chicha, Chui, and other nations of the southern Andes. They recall their military service to the Incas, who according to the memorial kept them as soldiers, free of other burdens, and their loyalty to the Spanish since the conquest, and they ask that their privileges be respected and their burdens eased: the mita of Potosí, the tribute, and the abuses of corregidores and doctrinal priests.

fuentes/memorial-de-charcas/por_que_impo.texto: It shows Indigenous lords using Castilian law to defend their interests and leaving a history of their region from their own point of view. It is a central source on the Aymara peoples of the south before and after the Incas.

fuentes/relacion-de-santillan/titulo.texto: Account of the Origin, Descent, Politics, and Government of the Incas

fuentes/relacion-de-santillan/soporte.texto: Manuscript account in response to a royal questionnaire; published by Marcos Jiménez de la Espada in Tres relaciones de antigüedades peruanas (1879)

fuentes/relacion-de-santillan/resumen.texto: Report by Hernando de Santillán, judge of the Audiencia of Lima, written in response to a Crown questionnaire about Inca tribute. It describes Inca government and taxation and denounces that after the conquest the Indians paid much more than before, that encomenderos, curacas, and their agents abused them, and that the population had fallen.

fuentes/relacion-de-santillan/por_que_im.texto: It is an example of criticism of colonization written from within the royal administration, and an early source on tribute and demographic decline.

fuentes/relacion-de-santillan/leer.0.tit.texto: In Tres relaciones de antigüedades peruanas (Madrid, 1879), on Internet Archive

fuentes/descripcion-de-vilcabamba-ocampo.texto: Description of the Province of San Francisco de la Victoria de Vilcabamba
Report addressed to the viceroy; translated into English by Clements Markham (1907)

Account by a Spanish resident of Vilcabamba, written almost forty years after the events, describing the province, its mines, and the campaign of 1572. As a witness, it recounts the entry of Túpac Amaru I into Cusco as a prisoner and his execution in the plaza, with the Indigenous crowd lamenting and the pleas for clemency from the clergy, and it records the words attributed to the Inca before he died.
It is the most detailed account of the execution of Túpac Amaru I, although it was written late.
English translation by Clements Markham (1907), together with Sarmiento’s History of the Incas, on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/gramatica-quechua-santo-tomas/ti.texto: Grammar or Art of the General Language of the Indians of the Kingdoms of Peru

fuentes/gramatica-quechua-santo-tomas/so.texto: Book printed in Valladolid by Francisco Fernández de Córdoba (1560)

fuentes/gramatica-quechua-santo-tomas/re.texto: First grammar of Quechua, published some twenty years after the author had been in Peru. It describes the language using the categories of Latin grammar and includes a doctrinal sermon in Quechua. In the prologue, dedicated to Philip II, it argues that Quechua is an orderly, rich, and elegant language, comparable to Latin, and that this proves the Indians are rational people with a political life.

fuentes/gramatica-quechua-santo-tomas/po.texto: It inaugurates the tradition of Andean grammars written by missionaries, and it is at the same time an argument for the capacity of the Indians, in the line of Las Casas.

fuentes/lexicon-quechua-santo-tomas/titu.texto: Lexicon or Vocabulary of the General Language of Peru

fuentes/lexicon-quechua-santo-tomas/sopo.texto: Book printed in Valladolid by Francisco Fernández de Córdoba (1560)

fuentes/lexicon-quechua-santo-tomas/resu.texto: First dictionary of Quechua, in two parts (Spanish-Quechua and Quechua-Spanish), published together with the same author’s grammar. It records above all the variety of the coast and central highlands that the author knew as a missionary, with many words from daily life, agriculture, and Andean institutions.

fuentes/lexicon-quechua-santo-tomas/por_.texto: It is the first printed description of the Quechua lexicon and a record of the language one generation after the conquest, before the Third Council of Lima adopted a norm closer to the Quechua of Cusco.

fuentes/vocabulario-gonzalez-holguin/tit.texto: Vocabulary of the General Language of All Peru Called Quichua or the Inca Language

fuentes/vocabulario-gonzalez-holguin/sop.texto: Book printed in Lima by Francisco del Canto (1608)

fuentes/vocabulario-gonzalez-holguin/res.texto: Quechua-Spanish and Spanish-Quechua dictionary of the Quechua of Cusco, compiled with the help of Cusco Indigenous informants over more than twenty years of work by the Jesuit. It records a very wide vocabulary, with terms for kinship, agriculture, religion, government, and emotional life, which allows the reconstruction of Andean concepts of the period.

fuentes/vocabulario-gonzalez-holguin/por.texto: It is the most complete dictionary of colonial Quechua and a central source for Andean history and anthropology.

fuentes/vocabulario-aymara-bertonio/sopo.texto: Book printed in Juli by Francisco del Canto (1612)

fuentes/vocabulario-aymara-bertonio/resu.texto: Aymara-Spanish and Spanish-Aymara dictionary by the Jesuit Ludovico Bertonio, printed at the Jesuit doctrina of Juli, on the shores of Lake Titicaca, together with a grammar of the language. It records the Aymara of the Lupaca of Chucuito, with the help of Indigenous collaborators, and includes terms for religion, social organization, and work.

fuentes/vocabulario-aymara-bertonio/por_.texto: It is the basis of later Aymara studies and a source on Lupaca society at the end of the 16th century.

fuentes/instruccion-de-albornoz/titulo.texto: Instruction for Discovering All the Guacas of Peru and Their Camayos and Haciendas

fuentes/instruccion-de-albornoz/soporte.texto: Manuscript; published by Pierre Duviols in 1967

fuentes/instruccion-de-albornoz/resumen.texto: Instruction by Cristóbal de Albornoz for priests and inspectors, with a long list of the main huacas of each province of Peru and of what had to be found out in order to discover them: their names, their servants, and their lands and livestock. Written by the inspector who had pursued the Taki Onqoy, it reflects the belief that the cult of the huacas was still organized and had to be dismantled.

fuentes/instruccion-de-albornoz/por_que_.texto: It is one of the first systematic guides to extirpation in Peru and an inventory of sixteenth-century Andean sacred places.

fuentes/extirpacion-de-la-idolatria-arri.texto: Extirpation of the Idolatry of Peru
Book printed in Lima by Jerónimo de Contreras (1621)

Manual by the Jesuit Arriaga for inspectors of idolatry, based on the campaigns of the archbishopric of Lima in 1616-1618, in which he took part. It describes in detail the huacas, the mummies of ancestors (mallquis), the amulets (conopas), the priests, and the festivals that were still alive half a century after the conquest, and it gives instructions for finding them, interrogating the peoples, and destroying the objects of worship. It includes accounts of what was burned and of the people punished.
It is both the instrument of a campaign of religious destruction and one of the best descriptions of Andean religion in the 17th century.

fuentes/visita-de-hernandez-principe/tit.texto: Idolatry Inspections of Ocros and Recuay

fuentes/visita-de-hernandez-principe/sop.texto: Reports by the inspector to the archbishop of Lima; published in the 20th century

fuentes/visita-de-hernandez-principe/res.texto: Reports by the priest and inspector of idolatry Rodrigo Hernández Príncipe on his visits to the villages of Ocros and Recuay, in the Áncash highlands, in 1621-1622. From the elders he collected the story of Tanta Carhua, a girl, daughter of the local curaca, who had been taken to Cusco and later sacrificed in a capacocha in Inca times, shut up alive in a tomb on a hilltop, and whose cult as protector of the village was still alive a century later. He also describes the mummies of the ancestors and the huacas of the ayllus that the inspector had destroyed.

fuentes/visita-de-hernandez-principe/por.texto: It is one of the few detailed accounts of a capacocha told from the community that gave up the victim, and it shows how the sacrifice brought prestige and offices to the girl’s lineage.

fuentes/apologetico-espinosa-medrano/tit.texto: Apology on Behalf of Don Luis de Góngora

fuentes/apologetico-espinosa-medrano/res.texto: Defense of Luis de Góngora’s poetry against the criticisms of the Portuguese writer Manuel de Faria e Sousa, written in Cusco by an Andean cleric of humble origin and published in Lima. It analyzes the poet’s language and figures with classical erudition and asserts the capacity of American men of letters to judge the literature of the metropolis.

fuentes/apologetico-espinosa-medrano/por.texto: It is the most important work of critical writing in Hispanic American Baroque, and it shows the level of literary life in colonial Cusco.

fuentes/apologetico-espinosa-medrano/lee.texto: Original edition (Lima, 1662), digitized by the Fundación Ignacio Larramendi, on Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-historica-juan-y-ulloa/.texto: Historical Account of the Voyage to South America
Four illustrated volumes, written with Antonio de Ulloa and printed in Madrid (1748), with a fifth on Astronomical and Physical Observations

Official account by Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa of their voyage with the French geodesic mission: Cartagena, Panama, Quito, Lima, and Chile. It describes the cities, the population and its castes, the obrajes and mines, the flora and fauna, the climate and volcanoes, with maps and engravings, and gives the first detailed European description of platinum.
It was one of the most complete descriptions of Spanish South America in the 18th century, and it was soon translated into several European languages.

fuentes/noticias-secretas-de-america/sop.texto: Confidential report by Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa for the Marquis of la Ensenada (around 1749); published in London in 1826 by David Barry under the title Noticias secretas de América

fuentes/noticias-secretas-de-america/res.texto: Confidential report by Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa on what they saw in Peru and Quito. It denounces smuggling, the corruption of corregidores and their forced distribution of goods, the abuses of doctrinal priests, obraje owners, and landowners against the Indians, forced labor, the disorder of the convents, and the enmity between Creoles and Peninsulars, and it proposes reforms for defense and government.

fuentes/noticias-secretas-de-america/por.texto: It is one of the harshest criticisms of the colonial regime written by officials of the Crown itself. Barry published it just as the republics had become independent and presented it as evidence against the Spanish government, so his edition must be read in that context.

fuentes/noticias-secretas-de-america/lee.texto: Madrid edition of 1918, volume 1, on Internet Archive

fuentes/nuevo-luciano-de-quito/soporte.texto: Manuscript dialogues that circulated in copies

fuentes/nuevo-luciano-de-quito/resumen.texto: Nine satirical dialogues in which Espejo criticizes the teaching of the Jesuits and of the religious orders in Quito, Baroque sacred oratory, scholasticism, and the ignorance of doctors and men of letters, and he proposes an education based on modern science, criticism, and good taste. It circulated in handwritten copies and earned him lasting enmities.

fuentes/nuevo-luciano-de-quito/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the earliest expressions of the Enlightenment in the Audiencia of Quito.

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-las-viruelas/t.texto: Reflections on a Safe Method to Protect Peoples from Smallpox

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-las-viruelas/s.texto: Memorandum written at the request of the cabildo of Quito

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-las-viruelas/r.texto: Memorandum written during a smallpox epidemic. Espejo proposes public hygiene measures, such as cleaning the streets, isolating the sick, and ventilating houses and hospitals; he argues that the disease is transmitted by living particles and criticizes the state of medicine and of the doctors of Quito.

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-las-viruelas/p.texto: It is the main medical text of the Audiencia of Quito in the 18th century and a precursor of Ecuadorian public health.

fuentes/primicias-de-la-cultura-de-quito.texto: First Fruits of the Culture of Quito
Newspaper; seven issues between January and March 1792

First newspaper of the Audiencia of Quito, published by Espejo as the organ of the Patriotic Society of Friends of the Country. In its seven issues it proposes the education of young people and the promotion of agriculture, industry, and the sciences, and it praises the talent of the people of Quito without openly attacking the government.
It marks the birth of journalism in present-day Ecuador and the spread of Enlightenment ideas in Quito.

fuentes/mercurio-peruano/autor.texto: Academic Society of Lovers of the Country of Lima

fuentes/mercurio-peruano/resumen.texto: Newspaper of the Society of Lovers of the Country of Lima, to which Hipólito Unanue, José Baquíjano y Carrillo, José Rossi y Rubí, and others contributed. It published studies on the geography, history, economy, mining, medicine, and customs of Peru, including articles on the Incas, the Amazonian missions, and Indigenous populations, with the aim of making the country known and promoting reforms.

fuentes/mercurio-peruano/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main publication of the Peruvian Enlightenment and one of the sources of the Creole consciousness of Peru as a homeland.

fuentes/mercurio-peruano/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume 1 (1791) of the original edition, on Internet Archive

fuentes/juan-santos-el-invencible/titulo.texto: Juan Santos, the Invincible: Manuscripts from 1742 to 1755

fuentes/juan-santos-el-invencible/soport.texto: Letters, reports, and statements by Franciscan missionaries, military officers, and viceregal authorities; compiled by Francisco A. Loayza (Lima, 1942)

fuentes/juan-santos-el-invencible/resume.texto: Documents of the period on the rebellion of Juan Santos Atahualpa: reports by the Franciscans of Ocopa and by military leaders, letters from the viceroys, and statements by witnesses. No written proclamation by Juan Santos himself survives; what is known of his message comes from what missionaries and witnesses who spoke with him or his followers reported, according to which he said he had come to recover the kingdom that the Spanish had taken from the Incas, asked that the Spanish and the Black people leave, and presented himself as a Christian.

fuentes/juan-santos-el-invencible/por_qu.texto: It is the documentary basis for what is known of the rebellion. Since it was written by its enemies, it must be read with care in order to reconstruct Juan Santos’s aims.

fuentes/carta-a-los-espanoles-americanos.texto: Written around 1791-1792; published in French in 1799 and in Spanish in London in 1801 by Francisco de Miranda

Appeal by the exiled Peruvian Jesuit to the Creoles to separate from Spain. It surveys three centuries of rule to argue that the descendants of the conquistadors were excluded from office, that the commercial monopoly impoverished America, and that the expulsion of the Jesuits showed the despotism of the Crown. It invokes the natural right to liberty and the example of the United States. It mentions the sufferings of the Indians, but the political subject is the “American Spaniards.”
It is one of the first manifestos of Spanish American independence, circulated by Miranda as propaganda for his project.

fuentes/flora-peruviana-et-chilensis/sop.texto: Three illustrated volumes, written with José Pavón and printed in Madrid (1798-1802), preceded by a Prodromus (1794)

fuentes/flora-peruviana-et-chilensis/res.texto: Botanical work by Hipólito Ruiz and José Pavón presenting the results of the expedition to Peru and Chile of 1777-1788. It describes and draws hundreds of species, many new to European science, with their medicinal and economic uses. It was left unfinished for lack of funds and because part of the collections was lost in a shipwreck and a fire.

fuentes/flora-peruviana-et-chilensis/por.texto: It is one of the great results of the Spanish Crown’s scientific expeditions in America.

fuentes/flora-peruviana-et-chilensis/lee.texto: Volume 1 (1798), copy from the Missouri Botanical Garden, on Internet Archive

fuentes/constitucion-quitena-1812/titulo.texto: Solemn Pact of Society and Union among the Provinces That Form the State of Quito

fuentes/constitucion-quitena-1812/autor.texto: Congress of the State of Quito

fuentes/constitucion-quitena-1812/resume.texto: Constitution of the State of Quito approved by a congress of deputies from the provinces of the Audiencia during the second Quito junta. It declares the State free and independent of any other government, although it recognizes Ferdinand VII as monarch if he is freed from French domination and respects the constitution; it establishes the separation of powers and the Catholic religion as the only one.

fuentes/constitucion-quitena-1812/por_qu.texto: It is the first constitution of present-day Ecuador and one of the first in Spanish America. It was in force for only a few months, until royalist troops took Quito at the end of 1812.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-bolivia.texto: Minutes of the assembly of representatives of Upper Peru (August 6, 1825)

Declaration approved in Chuquisaca by the assembly of deputies of the provinces of Upper Peru, called by Sucre after the defeat of the royalists. It proclaims the independence of those provinces from Spain and from any other nation and their constitution as a sovereign state. It was drafted by José Mariano Serrano, president of the assembly.
It is Bolivia’s founding act, and days later the country took the name Bolívar.

fuentes/hemming-conquest-of-the-incas/re.texto: Narrative history of the conquest of Peru from Pizarro’s arrival to the execution of Túpac Amaru I in 1572, based on Spanish and Indigenous chronicles and archival documents. It recounts the violence of the conquistadors and of the civil wars, the uprising of Manco Inca and the kingdom of Vilcabamba, and also the Andean divisions and the Indigenous allies that made the conquest possible.

fuentes/hemming-conquest-of-the-incas/po.texto: For decades it was the standard narrative synthesis on the conquest of Peru, and it fixed, with documents, dates such as that of Atahualpa’s execution.

fuentes/spanish-peru-lockhart/resumen.texto: Social history of the Spaniards of Peru in its first decades, based above all on notarial records. It shows that within a few years a complete society took shape, with encomenderos, stewards, artisans, merchants, Spanish women, enslaved Africans, and Indigenous people in the service of the Spaniards, rather than a camp of soldiers.

fuentes/spanish-peru-lockhart/por_que_im.texto: It renewed the history of the conquest by replacing the narrative of deeds with the study of ordinary people and their contracts.

fuentes/men-of-cajamarca/resumen.texto: Collective biography of the 168 Spaniards who captured Atahualpa and took part in the division of the ransom. It reconstructs their regional and social origins, their literacy, their trades, and their fates: most were neither nobles nor marginal figures but people of trades and middle classes, and many returned to Spain with their share.

fuentes/men-of-cajamarca/por_que_importa.texto: It dismantles both the heroic image and the image of a band of criminals, and it is a model of historical prosopography.

fuentes/los-cronistas-del-peru-porras/re.texto: Survey of the chroniclers of Peru, from those of the conquest to those of the 17th century, with a biography of each author, the context in which he wrote, his interests, his manuscripts and editions, and his value as a source. It resolved attributions such as that of The Conquest of Peru to Cristóbal de Mena.

fuentes/los-cronistas-del-peru-porras/po.texto: It remains the basic guide for reading Peruvian chronicles critically.

fuentes/vision-des-vaincus-wachtel/titul.texto: The Vision of the Vanquished: The Indians of Peru Facing the Spanish Conquest

fuentes/vision-des-vaincus-wachtel/resum.texto: Study of how the Andean peoples lived the conquest, based on Indigenous and mestizo chronicles, inspections, theatrical representations of Atahualpa’s death, and conquest dances. It proposes that the conquest produced a “destructuring” of the Andean world through demographic collapse, tribute, and the loss of religious meaning, and it analyzes Taki Onqoy and Vilcabamba as responses.

fuentes/vision-des-vaincus-wachtel/por_q.texto: It was the work that brought the perspective of the vanquished and historical anthropology into Andean history. Its critics noted that it underestimates the Andean capacity for adaptation and negotiation.

fuentes/los-huancas-aliados-de-la-conqui.texto: The Huancas, Allies of the Conquest
Article with documents in the Anales Científicos of the Universidad del Centro del Perú

Edition and study of three service records of Huanca curacas (1558, 1560, and 1561), with the lists of goods and people they handed over to the Spanish, read from their quipus. The author argues that the Huanca alliance, motivated by opposition to Inca rule, was decisive for the conquest of central Peru.
It opened the study of Indigenous allies of the conquest in the Andes, a line of research later extended to the Cañaris, Chachapoyas, and other peoples.

fuentes/transiciones-hacia-el-sistema-co.texto: Transitions to the Andean Colonial System
Book of essays (Instituto de Estudios Peruanos and El Colegio de México)

Essays on the passage from the Inca order to the colonial one: the role of the Andean economy in the silver of Potosí, the debate over the perpetuity of the encomiendas and the Crown’s calculations, and, in “The Great Vexation and Destruction of the Land,” the effect of the wars of conquest and the civil wars on the Andean population, which the author considers greater than was assumed.
It is a reference for understanding the conquest of Peru as a prolonged economic and political process, and not only as a series of battles.

fuentes/perus-indian-peoples-stern/titul.texto: Peru’s Indian Peoples and the Challenge of Spanish Conquest: Huamanga to 1640

fuentes/perus-indian-peoples-stern/resum.texto: Study of the Huamanga region from the conquest to 1640: the initial alliances of local lords with the Spanish, the crisis of the 1560s and Taki Onqoy, Toledo’s reforms and the mita, and the way Indigenous peoples used Spanish justice to defend themselves, a strategy that partly protected them but also tied them to the colonial system.

fuentes/perus-indian-peoples-stern/por_q.texto: It is a classic regional study that showed Indigenous people as actors who negotiated and litigated, not only as victims.

fuentes/huarochiri-spalding/titulo.texto: Huarochirí: An Andean Society under Inca and Spanish Rule

fuentes/huarochiri-spalding/resumen.texto: History of the province of Huarochirí, in the Lima highlands, from Inca rule to the 18th century: the organization of the ayllus and the curacas, the burdens of tribute, the mita and the repartimiento, the transformation of the curacas into intermediaries of the colonial order, and the rebellions, such as that of 1750.

fuentes/huarochiri-spalding/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the most cited long-term studies of an Andean society under colonial rule.

fuentes/miners-of-the-red-mountain/titul.texto: Miners of the Red Mountain: Indian Labor in Potosí, 1545-1650

fuentes/miners-of-the-red-mountain/resum.texto: Study of labor in the Potosí mines from their discovery to the mid-17th century. It shows that alongside the forced mitayos there was a growing mass of wage-earning Indigenous workers (mingas), often mitayos who stayed on, and that the mita functioned as a subsidy for mine owners.

fuentes/miners-of-the-red-mountain/por_q.texto: It qualified the image of Potosí as a mine worked only by forced labor, without denying the weight of the mita.

fuentes/the-potosi-mita-cole/resumen.texto: History of the Potosí mita from its organization by Toledo to 1700: the number of mitayos assigned and the number who actually arrived, the flight of Indigenous people from the obligated provinces, payment in silver to be exempted, viceroys’ reform projects such as that of the Duke of la Palata, and the moral debates over its legitimacy.

fuentes/the-potosi-mita-cole/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard study of the administration and decline of the mita in the 17th century.

fuentes/minas-de-huancavelica-lohmann/ti.texto: The Mines of Huancavelica in the 16th and 17th Centuries

fuentes/minas-de-huancavelica-lohmann/re.texto: History of the Huancavelica mercury mine since its discovery: the contracts between the Crown and the guild of miners, the mita assigned to the mine, production, the transport of mercury to Potosí, and the working and health conditions of the mitayos, documented in the complaints of viceroys, clergy, and officials.

fuentes/minas-de-huancavelica-lohmann/po.texto: It is the basic documentary study of the mine that made the silver of Potosí possible.

fuentes/huancavelica-mercury-mine-whitak.texto: Study of the Huancavelica mine in the 18th century, focused on the Bourbon attempts to increase production and reform its administration, on the conflicts between governors and miners, such as those involving Antonio de Ulloa, and on the decline of the mine at the end of the colonial period.
It was the first study in English of the mine, and it remains a reference for the 18th century.

fuentes/servicio-personal-zavala/titulo.texto: The Personal Service of the Indians in Peru

fuentes/servicio-personal-zavala/resumen.texto: Legal and administrative history of Indigenous labor in Peru: the services of the encomienda, the mining and town mita, the yanaconas, and work in obrajes and chacras, with the Crown’s legislation, the orders of viceroys and audiencias, and reports on how they were applied.

fuentes/servicio-personal-zavala/por_que.texto: It gathers and organizes the documentation on forced labor in Peru and makes it possible to compare what the law required with what was practiced.

fuentes/lutte-contre-les-religions-autoc.texto: The Struggle against Native Religions in Colonial Peru

History of the policy of the Church and the Crown against Andean religion, from the destruction of temples during the conquest to the large campaigns of extirpation in the archbishopric of Lima. It shows, among other things, that the campaign begun by Francisco de Ávila in 1609 arose after his parishioners in Huarochirí denounced him before the ecclesiastical court for abuses.
It is the foundational work on the study of the extirpation of idolatries as a historical policy with concrete interests.

fuentes/idolatry-and-its-enemies/titulo.texto: Idolatry and Its Enemies: Colonial Andean Religion and Extirpation, 1640-1750

fuentes/idolatry-and-its-enemies/resumen.texto: Study based on the case files of idolatry trials of the archbishopric of Lima. It shows that the Andean religion of the 17th century was neither an intact survival nor a vanished tradition, but combined the cult of huacas and ancestors with Christian practices, and that the trials also reflect local conflicts among priests, curacas, and villages.

fuentes/idolatry-and-its-enemies/por_que.texto: It changed the picture of extirpation from a clash between two separate religions to a process of religious mixing and negotiation.

fuentes/el-retorno-de-las-huacas/titulo.texto: The Return of the Huacas: Studies and Documents on the Taki Onqoy, 16th Century

fuentes/el-retorno-de-las-huacas/resumen.texto: Edition of the service records of Cristóbal de Albornoz and other documents on the Taki Onqoy, with studies by several authors. It gathers the documentary basis of the debate over the movement: whether it was a millenarian religious rebellion against Spanish rule or whether its scope was enlarged by the inspector who pursued it.

fuentes/el-retorno-de-las-huacas/por_que.texto: It is the main edition of the sources on the Taki Onqoy.

fuentes/vertical-empire-mumford/titulo.texto: Vertical Empire: The General Resettlement of Indians in the Colonial Andes

fuentes/vertical-empire-mumford/resumen.texto: Study of the general resettlement ordered by Viceroy Toledo: its intellectual antecedents in the idea of urban “policía” and in the knowledge of the Inca order gathered by officials, its implementation by inspectors and curacas, and its results, which were more limited than the viceroy intended, with many Indigenous people returning to their former settlements.

fuentes/vertical-empire-mumford/por_que_.texto: It is the most complete study of one of the largest forced reorganizations of population in the 16th century.

fuentes/la-sal-de-los-cerros/titulo.texto: Salt of the Hills: An Approach to the Campa World

fuentes/la-sal-de-los-cerros/resumen.texto: Ethnohistory of the Asháninka (called campas by the Spanish) of the central Peruvian rainforest, of their exchange relations with the highlands, centered on the salt of the Cerro de la Sal, and of their history of contact with missionaries and settlers. It devotes a central study to the rebellion of Juan Santos Atahualpa, which it interprets as a defense of territory and of their own order against the missions.

fuentes/la-sal-de-los-cerros/por_que_imp.texto: It is the foundational work on the Asháninka and on the rebellion of Juan Santos.

fuentes/rebellions-and-revolts-ophelan/t.texto: Rebellions and Revolts in Eighteenth-Century Peru and Upper Peru

fuentes/rebellions-and-revolts-ophelan/r.texto: Catalogue and analysis of more than a hundred revolts and rebellions of the 18th century in Peru and Upper Peru, from local riots against corregidores to the great rebellion of 1780-1781. It links their increase to fiscal pressure: the legalization of the forced distribution of goods in the mid-century and the Bourbon reforms of the alcabala and customs.

fuentes/rebellions-and-revolts-ophelan/p.texto: It is the quantitative basis for the discussion of the causes of the Andean rebellions of the 18th century.

fuentes/tupac-amaru-rebellion-walker/res.texto: Narrative history of the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II and Micaela Bastidas, from Tinta in 1780 to the negotiations and repression of 1781-1783. It describes the violence on both sides, the role of the caciques who fought on behalf of the Crown, and the harshness of the punishments that followed.

fuentes/tupac-amaru-rebellion-walker/por.texto: It is the most recent and best-documented synthesis of the rebellion.

fuentes/we-alone-will-rule/titulo.texto: We Alone Will Rule: Native Andean Politics in the Age of Insurgency

fuentes/we-alone-will-rule/resumen.texto: Study of the politics of the Aymara communities of the La Paz region in the 18th century: the crisis of hereditary cacicazgo, the conflicts of the communities with their caciques and corregidores, and the insurrection of Túpac Katari in 1781, which the author interprets as a project of Indigenous self-government.

fuentes/we-alone-will-rule/por_que_impor.texto: It renewed the history of the Aymara rebellion of 1781 from the standpoint of communal politics.

fuentes/shadows-of-empire-garrett/titulo.texto: Shadows of Empire: The Indian Nobility of Cusco, 1750-1825

fuentes/shadows-of-empire-garrett/resume.texto: Study of the Indigenous nobility of Cusco and its bishopric in the last colonial century: its wealth, its cacicazgos, its education at the San Borja college, and its stance toward the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II, which much of it opposed. It analyzes its decline after the rebellion, when the Crown distrusted all Indigenous authority.

fuentes/shadows-of-empire-garrett/por_qu.texto: It shows that colonial Indigenous society had elites with their own interests, often opposed to one another.

fuentes/kingdom-of-quito-andrien/resumen.texto: Economic and political history of the Audiencia of Quito in its last century and a half: the crisis of the highland textile obrajes in the face of European competition, the boom of Guayaquil cacao, the Bourbon reforms and the 1765 revolt of the barrios, and the regional tensions that weighed on independence.

fuentes/kingdom-of-quito-andrien/por_que.texto: It explains the economic foundations of Ecuador’s regional division between the highlands and the coast.

fuentes/quito-1599-lane/titulo.texto: Quito 1599: City and Colony in Transition

fuentes/quito-1599-lane/resumen.texto: Portrait of the Audiencia of Quito around 1599: southern gold mining, the obrajes, epidemics, the revolt over the alcabalas, the lives of women and enslaved Africans, and the negotiation with the cimarrones of Esmeraldas, whose portrait of 1599 gives the book its title.

fuentes/quito-1599-lane/por_que_importa.texto: It is a vivid social history of a colonial Andean city, built from judicial and notarial case files.

fuentes/african-slave-in-colonial-peru/t.texto: The African Slave in Colonial Peru, 1524-1650

fuentes/african-slave-in-colonial-peru/r.texto: Study of African slavery in Peru during the first colonial century: the slave trade routes through Cartagena and Panama, prices and the number of enslaved people, their work in Lima, on the haciendas, and in trades, the legislation, the Church, the confraternities, manumission, and the free population of African origin.

fuentes/african-slave-in-colonial-peru/p.texto: It was the first comprehensive study of the African population of colonial Peru, which came to be nearly half of Lima’s.

fuentes/shaky-colonialism/titulo.texto: Shaky Colonialism: The 1746 Earthquake and Tsunami in Lima and Callao

fuentes/shaky-colonialism/resumen.texto: History of the 1746 earthquake and tsunami and of the reconstruction of Lima: the dead, the destruction of Callao, the religious interpretations of the disaster, and Viceroy Manso de Velasco’s attempts to reform the city, which clashed with the Church and the elites, and the fear of an Indigenous rebellion that led to the repression of the conspiracy of 1750.

fuentes/shaky-colonialism/por_que_import.texto: It uses a natural disaster to study how colonial power worked in Lima.

fuentes/repartos-forzosos-moreno-cebrian.texto: The Corregidor de Indios and the Peruvian Economy in the Eighteenth Century: The Forced Distribution of Goods

Study of the corregidor de indios and of the forced distribution of goods in eighteenth-century Peru: the purchase of offices, the credit of Lima merchants, the tariffs with which the Crown legalized the distribution in the mid-century, and the abuses denounced by officials and communities until its abolition.
It is the standard study of one of the main causes of the Andean rebellions of the 18th century.

fuentes/mission-culture-upper-amazon/tit.texto: Mission Culture on the Upper Amazon: Native Tradition, Jesuit Enterprise, and Secular Politics in Moxos, 1660-1880

fuentes/mission-culture-upper-amazon/res.texto: History of the Moxos missions: the Indigenous societies of the plains, the founding of the Jesuit missions from 1682, their cattle-raising and craft economy, the epidemics, the government of the Indigenous cabildos, and what happened after the expulsion of the Jesuits, including civil administration and commercial exploitation in the 19th century.

fuentes/mission-culture-upper-amazon/por.texto: It shows the missions as a joint construction of Jesuits and Indigenous peoples, with benefits and costs for the latter.

fuentes/historia-de-la-pintura-cuzquena/.texto: José de Mesa and Teresa Gisbert

History of colonial Cusco painting, from the European painters of the 16th century to the Indigenous and mestizo workshops of the 18th, with biographies, catalogues of works, and a study of the separation of Indigenous painters from the guild in 1688 and of the serial production of paintings for the whole viceroyalty.
It is the reference work on the Cusco school.

fuentes/qaraqara-charka/titulo.texto: Qaraqara-Charka: Mallku, Inka, and King in the Province of Charcas (15th-17th Centuries)

fuentes/qaraqara-charka/autor.texto: Tristan Platt, Thérèse Bouysse-Cassagne, and Olivia Harris

fuentes/qaraqara-charka/soporte.texto: Book with documents (Institut français d’études andines and Plural)

fuentes/qaraqara-charka/resumen.texto: History of the federation of the Qaraqaras and the Charkas in the southern Andes, based on a large body of documents published in the book, including the Memorial de Charcas and the service records of their lords. It reconstructs their political and military organization, their relations with the Incas, and their negotiations with the Spanish.

fuentes/qaraqara-charka/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main edition and study of the sources on the southern Aymara lordships during the colonial transition.

fuentes/religion-in-the-andes/titulo.texto: Religion in the Andes: Vision and Imagination in Early Colonial Peru

fuentes/religion-in-the-andes/resumen.texto: Study of how chroniclers, missionaries, and Andean and mestizo authors understood Andean religion from the conquest to Garcilaso, using the categories of classical philosophy and Christian theology, and of how those interpretations shaped evangelization and extirpation policy.

fuentes/religion-in-the-andes/por_que_im.texto: It is a key work for reading Andean religious sources in their intellectual context.

fuentes/domination-without-dominance/tit.texto: Domination without Dominance: Inca-Spanish Encounters in Early Colonial Peru

fuentes/domination-without-dominance/res.texto: Study of the first years of the conquest, from Cajamarca to Manco Inca’s uprising. It argues that the Spanish did not control the situation: they depended on alliances with Inca factions and Andean peoples who had their own aims, and that the image of a rapid and total domination is a construction of later chronicles.

fuentes/domination-without-dominance/por.texto: It is part of the revision that questions the account of a conquest carried out by a few Spaniards.

personas/francisco-pizarro/resumen.texto: Conquistador born in Trujillo (Extremadura), the natural son of a hidalgo, who reached America around 1502 and was with Balboa when the Pacific was sighted. Partnered with Diego de Almagro and Hernando de Luque, he explored the southern Pacific coast from 1524, obtained the Capitulación de Toledo (1529) from the Crown, and in 1532 captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca. He founded Lima in 1535 and governed New Castile until partisans of Almagro el Mozo killed him in 1541.

personas/diego-de-almagro/resumen.texto: Conquistador born in Almagro (Castile), Pizarro's partner from 1524 and in charge of supplying the expeditions from Panama. In 1534 the Crown gave him the governorship of New Toledo, south of Pizarro's, and the dispute over Cusco led to war between the two factions. His expedition to Chile (1535-1537) was the first European entry into what is now northwestern Argentina: it passed through Tupiza, the old Chicoana and El Shincal, and crossed the Andes in the autumn of 1536. On his return he took Cusco, was defeated at Las Salinas in 1538 and Hernando Pizarro had him executed.

personas/hernando-pizarro/resumen.texto: The only legitimate son of the father of the Pizarros. He was at Cajamarca, plundered the sanctuary of Pachacamac in 1533, and took the royal fifth of Atahualpa’s ransom to Spain. He withstood the siege of Cusco (1536-1537), defeated Almagro at Las Salinas, and had him executed; for this reason, back in Spain, he spent about twenty years imprisoned in the castle of La Mota in Medina del Campo.

personas/gonzalo-pizarro/resumen.texto: Younger half-brother of Francisco Pizarro. He took part in the conquest and the siege of Cusco, led the expedition of the Cinnamon Land east of Quito in 1541-1542, from which Orellana broke away, and in 1544 headed the encomenderos who rejected the New Laws. He governed Peru after defeating Viceroy Núñez Vela at Iñaquito (1546), until La Gasca defeated him at Jaquijahuana and had him beheaded in 1548.

personas/juan-pizarro/resumen.texto: Half-brother of Francisco Pizarro. He governed Cusco with Gonzalo in 1535-1536; chroniclers, among them his cousin Pedro Pizarro and Titu Cusi himself, recount how the two brothers imprisoned and humiliated Manco Inca to extract gold from him. He died from a stone blow to the head during the assault on Sacsayhuamán, in the siege of Cusco.

personas/diego-de-almagro-el-mozo/resume.texto: Mestizo son of Diego de Almagro and an Indigenous woman from Panama. Supporters of his father, impoverished after Las Salinas, killed Francisco Pizarro in Lima in 1541 and proclaimed him governor; he was defeated by Cristóbal Vaca de Castro at Chupas (1542) and beheaded in Cusco.

personas/hernando-de-luque/resumen.texto: Cleric from Panama, partner of Pizarro and Almagro in the Peru enterprise from 1524, to which he contributed his own money or that of third parties. The Capitulación de Toledo named him bishop of Tumbes and protector of the Indians, but he died in 1532 without reaching Peru.

personas/vicente-de-valverde/resumen.texto: Dominican who accompanied Pizarro. At Cajamarca he was the one who went ahead to speak with Atahualpa, holding a religious book; according to the Spanish witnesses, the Inca threw it to the ground, and that preceded the attack. He was the first bishop of Cusco (1537), and he was killed by the Indigenous people of Puná Island in 1541, as he was leaving Peru after Pizarro’s death.

personas/felipillo/resumen.texto: A young Indigenous man from the northern coast, taken by Pizarro in 1528 to learn Castilian, who served as interpreter at Cajamarca and in the trial of Atahualpa. Several later chroniclers, among them Garcilaso, accuse him of distorting the Inca's words; those accusations come second-hand and cannot be verified. According to the chroniclers, Almagro had him executed during the expedition to Chile.

personas/francisco-de-xerez/resumen.texto: A native of Seville, secretary to Francisco Pizarro from the 1524 expedition and notary at Cajamarca, where he recorded the division of Atahualpa's ransom. He returned to Spain in 1533 with his share and in 1534 published in Seville the True Account of the Conquest of Peru, the official chronicle of the conquest.

personas/cristobal-de-mena/resumen.texto: A captain under Pizarro at Cajamarca, born in Ciudad Real. Dissatisfied with his share of the ransom, he returned to Spain in 1533; he is credited with The Conquest of Peru, Called New Castile, published anonymously in Seville in April 1534, the first printed chronicle of the conquest.

personas/pedro-pizarro/resumen.texto: A cousin of Francisco Pizarro, he came to Peru as a page and was present at Cajamarca, the siege of Cusco and the civil wars. An encomendero and vecino of Arequipa, he completed there in 1571 his Account of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru, one of the most detailed firsthand accounts of the conquest.

personas/agustin-de-zarate/resumen.texto: Accountant of the Royal Treasury who arrived in Peru in 1544 with Viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela to audit the accounts of the conquest. He lived through the rebellion of Gonzalo Pizarro, which forced him to serve him, and after returning to Spain published in Antwerp in 1555 the History of the Discovery and Conquest of Peru.

personas/sebastian-de-belalcazar/resumen.texto: Andalusian conquistador who was at Cajamarca and, as Pizarro's lieutenant in San Miguel de Piura, marched north in 1534 over the northern Tawantinsuyu with Cañari allies, defeated Rumiñahui and occupied Quito. He moved further north, founded Cali (1536) and Popayán (1537), reached the savanna of Bogotá in 1539, where he met Jiménez de Quesada and Federmann, and became governor of Popayán; he died in Cartagena de Indias in 1551, condemned for the execution of his rival Jorge Robledo.

personas/cristobal-vaca-de-castro/resume.texto: Judge of the Audiencia of Valladolid sent by Charles V in 1540 as a magistrate to mediate between the Pizarristas and the Almagristas. On learning of Pizarro's death he took over the government, defeated Almagro the Younger at Chupas (1542), and governed until the arrival of Viceroy Núñez Vela; accused of enriching himself in office, he was imprisoned in Spain for several years and later rehabilitated.

personas/francisco-de-carvajal/resumen.texto: A veteran soldier of the Italian Wars who was field master of Gonzalo Pizarro during the encomenderos' rebellion. Chroniclers, beginning with Zárate and Diego Fernández, credit him with hundreds of hangings of enemies, and called him the “demon of the Andes.” He was hanged and quartered after Jaquijahuana, at over eighty years of age.

personas/francisco-hernandez-giron/resum.texto: An encomendero of Cusco who in 1553 rose up against the Audiencia of Lima when the abolition of personal service of the Indians was enforced. He raised an army that included African slaves, whom he promised freedom, won at Chuquinga, and was defeated at Pucará in 1554; he was executed in Lima. It was the last major rebellion of the encomenderos.

personas/martin-garcia-onez-de-loyola/re.texto: A captain from Guipúzcoa, a great-nephew of Ignatius of Loyola, who came to Peru with Viceroy Toledo and in 1572 captured Túpac Amaru I in the forest of Vilcabamba. As a reward he married Beatriz Clara Coya, heir of Sayri Túpac. He was governor of Chile and died in the Mapuche ambush at Curalaba in 1598.

personas/lope-garcia-de-castro/resumen.texto: Jurist of the Council of the Indies who governed Peru as president of the Audiencia of Lima from 1564 to 1569. He created the corregimientos of Indians (1565) and negotiated with Titu Cusi the Capitulation of Acobamba (1566); the Instruction that the Inca of Vilcabamba issued in 1570 is addressed to him.

personas/francisco-de-borja-y-aragon/res.texto: Prince of Esquilache, viceroy of Peru from 1615 to 1621, and a poet. He supported the campaigns to extirpate idolatry of the archdiocese of Lima, for which a house of confinement for Indigenous “dogmatizers” was opened in the Cercado, and he ordered the founding of colleges for the sons of caciques in Lima (the Colegio del Príncipe) and in Cusco (San Francisco de Borja).

personas/jose-antonio-manso-de-velasco/r.texto: Count of Superunda, viceroy of Peru from 1745 to 1761, after governing Chile (1737-1744), where he founded towns such as San Felipe, Los Ángeles, Talca, Rancagua, Curicó and Copiapó. He directed the reconstruction of Lima and Callao after the earthquake and tsunami of 1746, had the Real Felipe fortress built, and faced the rebellion of Juan Santos Atahualpa and the conspiracy of Lima and Huarochirí of 1750.

personas/jose-antonio-de-areche/resumen.texto: Jurist sent by Charles III as visitador general of Peru (1777-1782) to apply the Bourbon reforms: he raised the alcabala, set up customs houses and tightened tax collection. In 1781 he handed down the sentence against Túpac Amaru II and his family, which also banned the dress, portraits and noble titles of the Inca nobility.

personas/jose-fernando-de-abascal/resume.texto: Viceroy of Peru from 1806 to 1816. He made Lima the center of the royalist reaction: he sent troops against the juntas of Quito, Upper Peru and Chile, and against the rebellion of Cusco of 1814. He supported smallpox vaccination and founded the General Cemetery and the College of Medicine of San Fernando of Lima.

personas/manco-inca/resumen.texto: Son of Huayna Cápac, who sided with the Spanish against Atahualpa's generals and was made Inca by Pizarro in Cusco in 1533. Mistreated and extorted by the Pizarro brothers, he escaped in 1536 and led the great uprising that besieged Cusco and sent an army against Lima; defeated, he withdrew to Vilcabamba, from where he kept attacking roads and towns allied with the Spanish. Almagrist refugees at his court killed him at Vitcos in 1544.

personas/titu-cusi-yupanqui/resumen.texto: Son of Manco Inca, he governed the State of Vilcabamba from 1560 to 1571. He negotiated the Capitulation of Acobamba (1566), accepted baptism (1568) and the presence of Augustinian friars, and in 1570 issued an Instruction, put into Castilian by a friar and a mestizo, which is the most direct Inca version of the conquest. He died of a sudden illness; his captains blamed and killed Fray Diego Ortiz.

personas/tupac-amaru-i/resumen.texto: Son of Manco Inca and last Inca of Vilcabamba, successor of Titu Cusi in 1571. After the Incas killed a Spanish envoy, Viceroy Toledo declared war: Spanish troops and their Indigenous allies took Vilcabamba, and Martín García de Loyola captured him in the forest. He was tried in Cusco and beheaded in the plaza on September 24, 1572, despite pleas for clemency from clerics and residents.

personas/sayri-tupac/resumen.texto: Son of Manco Inca, Inca of Vilcabamba from his father's death. In 1558 he agreed to go out to Lima after negotiating with Viceroy Cañete: he gave up his rights in exchange for a pardon, baptism and a large encomienda in the Yucay valley. He died there in 1561; his daughter Beatriz Clara Coya inherited his property.

personas/paullu-inca/resumen.texto: Son of Huayna Cápac who chose to ally with the Spanish: he accompanied Almagro to Chile, fought against his brother Manco, and the Spanish recognized him as Inca in Cusco. Baptized as Cristóbal, he received encomiendas and kept part of the prestige of the Inca nobility, which he passed on to his descendants in colonial Cusco.

personas/cura-ocllo/resumen.texto: Sister and wife of Manco Inca. Captured during Gonzalo Pizarro's entry into Vilcabamba in 1539, she was killed at Yucay on Francisco Pizarro's orders as a reprisal against Manco: according to the chroniclers, she was tied to a post, shot to death with arrows, and her body thrown into the river so that the Incas would find it.

personas/rumi-nahui/resumen.texto: General of Atahualpa who escaped from Cajamarca with part of the army and, after the Inca's death, organized the defense of the north against the Spanish and their Cañari allies. The chronicles accuse him of killing relatives of Atahualpa and of burning Quito before abandoning it; defeated in 1534, he was captured and executed in 1535. In republican Ecuador he was made a national hero.

personas/francisco-chilche/resumen.texto: Cañari curaca taken to Cusco in Inca times, who allied with Pizarro and was captain of the Cañari auxiliaries during the siege of Cusco in 1536-1537. He governed the Yucay valley in the name of the Spanish; in 1561 he was imprisoned on suspicion of poisoning Sayri Túpac, although this was never proven.

personas/beatriz-clara-coya/resumen.texto: Daughter of Sayri Túpac and heir to his encomiendas in Yucay. Viceroy Toledo arranged her marriage to Martín García de Loyola, captor of Túpac Amaru I; a colonial painting in the Compañía church in Cusco presents that wedding as an alliance between the Inca nobility and the lineages of Loyola and Borja.

personas/juan-santos-atahualpa/resumen.texto: An Indigenous man or mestizo from the highlands, apparently from Cusco, who in 1742 appeared in the central jungle of Peru presenting himself as a descendant of Atahualpa and as an Inca. He led an uprising of Asháninka, Yanesha and other peoples that drove out the Franciscans and the colonists of the region; viceregal troops failed to defeat him. When and how he died is unknown.

personas/alonso-de-illescas/resumen.texto: An enslaved African who, according to the accounts of the time, was born in Cape Verde and raised in Seville, and who reached the coast of Esmeraldas in 1553 after the shipwreck of the vessel carrying him from Panama to Peru. With other survivors he imposed himself on the Indigenous peoples of the area, formed with them a mixed population, and negotiated with the Audiencia of Quito, which could not subdue him by force of arms.

personas/mateo-pumacahua/resumen.texto: Cacique of Chinchero, from the Indigenous nobility of Cusco, who fought on the royalist side in 1780-1781 against Túpac Amaru II and later against the insurgents of Upper Peru. In 1814 he joined the rebellion of the Angulo brothers in Cusco; defeated at Umachiri in 1815, he was executed.

personas/domingo-de-santo-tomas/resumen.texto: A Dominican from Seville who arrived in Peru around 1540, learned the Quechua of the central coast and in 1560 published the first grammar and the first vocabulary of that language. An ally of Las Casas, he denounced the abuses of the encomenderos and around 1560-1562 supported the curacas' offer to prevent the perpetuity of the encomiendas; he was bishop of La Plata (Charcas) from 1563.

personas/jeronimo-de-loayza/resumen.texto: Dominican, first bishop and first archbishop of Lima. He presided over the first two Lima councils (1551-1552 and 1567-1568), which ordered that Indians be taught the catechism in their own language, and in 1549 he founded the hospital of Santa Ana for Indigenous people.

personas/santa-rosa-de-lima/resumen.texto: Isabel Flores de Oliva, a native of Lima from a modest Creole family, a Dominican tertiary known for her penances and visions. Canonized in 1671, she was the first saint born in the Americas; her cult, promoted by the Crown and the Dominicans, became a symbol of Creole pride, and she is the patron saint of Lima, of the Americas and of the Philippines.

personas/martin-de-porres/resumen.texto: Son of a gentleman from Burgos and of a freedwoman of African origin, he entered the Dominican convent of the Rosary in Lima as a donado, where he attended the infirmary and the poor and enslaved; he professed as a lay brother in 1603. Canonized in 1962, he is the most popular saint in Peru.

personas/diego-gonzalez-holguin/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Cáceres who came to Peru in 1581 and worked in Cusco and Juli. He published in Lima a grammar (1607) and a vocabulary (1608) of the Quechua of Cusco, still considered the best dictionary of colonial Quechua.

personas/ludovico-bertonio/resumen.texto: Italian Jesuit who worked for almost thirty years in the doctrina of Juli, beside Lake Titicaca, among the Lupaca. In Juli in 1612 he published a grammar and a vocabulary of the Aymara language, the basis of later studies of that language.

personas/pablo-jose-de-arriaga/resumen.texto: Basque Jesuit, rector of colleges in Lima and Arequipa, who accompanied as a missionary the visitations to extirpate idolatry in the archdiocese of Lima in 1616-1618. In 1621 he published The Extirpation of Idolatry in Peru, a manual for visitors. He died in a shipwreck off Cuba on his way to Spain.

personas/cristobal-de-albornoz/resumen.texto: Cleric of the Cusco cathedral who, as ecclesiastical visitor, toured the provinces of Huamanga, Parinacochas and Soras around 1569-1571 pursuing the Taki Onqoy movement. His service reports, written to obtain promotions, are the main source on that movement; he also wrote an instruction for uncovering huacas.

personas/antonio-ricardo/resumen.texto: Printer from Turin who worked in Mexico and went to Lima in 1580 with the Jesuits. In 1584 he printed the Doctrina christiana of the Third Council, the first book printed in South America, and he kept printing works in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara until his death.

personas/juan-de-espinosa-medrano/resume.texto: Cleric and preacher from Cusco of humble origins, nicknamed “the Lunarejo,” professor at the seminary of San Antonio Abad. He wrote the Apologetic in Favor of Góngora (Lima, 1662), sermons and sacramental plays in Quechua, and is one of the great figures of the Andean Baroque.

personas/diego-quispe-tito/resumen.texto: Indigenous painter from Cusco, from a noble family, one of the leading figures of the Cusco school. He worked from Flemish engravings that he adapted with landscapes, birds and Andean details, as in the Zodiac series of the Cusco cathedral (1681).

personas/bernardo-bitti/resumen.texto: Italian Jesuit brother and painter, trained in Mannerism, who arrived in Lima in 1575 and painted for Jesuit churches in Lima, Cusco, Juli, Arequipa, La Paz and Potosí. His style was one of the initial models for Andean painters.

personas/miguel-de-santiago/resumen.texto: Painter from Quito, one of the leading figures of the 17th-century Quito school. He painted, among other works, the series on the life of Saint Augustine for the Augustinian convent in Quito, based on European engravings, and works for the sanctuary of Guápulo.

personas/caspicara/resumen.texto: Indigenous sculptor from Quito, one of the best-known figures of the 18th-century Quito school. His polychrome wooden carvings for the city's churches show the work of the Indigenous and mestizo workshops that supplied images to much of Spanish America.

personas/samuel-fritz/resumen.texto: Bohemian Jesuit who from 1686 worked as a missionary among the Omagua and other peoples of the Amazon, in the Maynas missions. He drew the first detailed map of the course of the Amazon, engraved in Quito in 1707, and defended Spanish jurisdiction over the river against the Portuguese of Pará.

personas/cipriano-barace/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Navarre, one of the founders of the Moxos missions in the lowlands of eastern Bolivia, where he founded Trinidad in 1686 and learned the Moxo language. He was killed in 1702 by the Baure, whom he was trying to evangelize.

personas/martin-schmid/resumen.texto: Swiss Jesuit who worked in the Chiquitos missions between 1730 and the expulsion of 1767. He built the churches of San Rafael, San Javier and Concepción, today World Heritage Sites, and organized workshops for instruments and music in which the Chiquitano people played and copied Baroque music.

personas/jorge-juan/resumen.texto: Naval officer and mathematician from Alicante who, with Antonio de Ulloa, accompanied the French geodesic mission in the Audiencia of Quito (1736-1744). With Ulloa he wrote the Historical Account of the Voyage to South America (1748) and the confidential report later published as Secret News of America; afterward he reformed Spanish shipbuilding.

personas/antonio-de-ulloa/resumen.texto: Naval officer and naturalist from Seville who, with Jorge Juan, took part in the Spanish portion of the geodesic mission in Quito, and co-authored the Historical Account (1748), where platinum is described, and the Secret News. He later served as governor of Huancavelica (1758-1764), where he clashed with the miners, and as the first Spanish governor of Louisiana (1766-1768).

personas/pedro-vicente-maldonado/resumen.texto: Scientist born in Riobamba who collaborated with the French geodesic mission and, as governor of Esmeraldas, opened a road from Quito to the coast. His map of the province of Quito, published in 1750, was the most accurate map of the region in its time. He died in London in 1748.

personas/eugenio-espejo/resumen.texto: Physician, writer and journalist from Quito of humble origins, with Indigenous ancestry according to most of his biographers. He criticized the teaching and customs of Quito in The New Lucian (1779), wrote on the prevention of smallpox (1785), and in 1792 published First Fruits of the Culture of Quito, the first newspaper of the Audiencia. Accused of seditious writings, he died in 1795 shortly after leaving prison.

personas/hipolito-unanue/resumen.texto: Physician and naturalist born in Arica, a member of the Society of Friends of the Country and one of the main contributors to the Peruvian Mercury. He promoted the anatomy theater and the College of Medicine of San Fernando of Lima, wrote about the climate of Lima (1806), and was a minister under San Martín and Bolívar.

personas/juan-pablo-viscardo/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Pampacolca (Arequipa), expelled with his order in 1767 and exiled in Italy. He went to London, offered the British government plans to emancipate Spanish America, and wrote the Letter to the Spanish Americans, which Francisco de Miranda published after his death.

personas/hipolito-ruiz/resumen.texto: Pharmacist and botanist who, with José Pavón, directed the botanical expedition to Peru and Chile (1777-1788). He collected and described hundreds of plants new to European science, among them several species of cinchona, and published with Pavón the Flora peruviana et chilensis.

personas/juan-pio-montufar/resumen.texto: Marquis of Selva Alegre, a Creole aristocrat of Quito and a patron of Espejo. He presided over the Sovereign Junta formed in Quito on August 10, 1809, which deposed the president of the Audiencia while swearing loyalty to Ferdinand VII; after its fall he was persecuted and died in exile in Spain.

hechos/sociedad-de-pizarro-almagro-y-luq.texto: Partnership of Pizarro, Almagro and Luque

Around 1524, in Panama, Francisco Pizarro, Diego de Almagro and the cleric Hernando de Luque formed a partnership to explore and conquer the southern lands from which news had arrived, with money from Luque and other investors. Like most conquests, it was a private enterprise: the partners put up the capital and shared the spoils, while the Crown granted the titles and reserved the quinto.

hechos/viajes-de-pizarro-al-peru/resumen.texto: On two voyages from Panama (1524-1525 and 1526-1528), Pizarro and Almagro explored the Pacific coast to the south, facing hunger, disease and clashes with coastal peoples. On the second, the pilot Bartolomé Ruiz captured a raft of merchants from the Ecuadorian coast loaded with textiles and metals, and on Gallo Island thirteen men stayed with Pizarro when the governor of Panama ordered the return; the scene of the line drawn in the sand is recounted by later chroniclers. In 1528 they reached Tumbes, the first city of the Tawantinsuyu they saw, and Pizarro traveled to Spain to ask for the conquest.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-miguel-de-piura/.texto: Founding of San Miguel de Piura

In 1532, before marching on Cajamarca, Pizarro founded San Miguel in the Tangarará valley, the first Spanish city in present-day Peru, where he left the sick and distributed the Indians of the area among the residents. The city moved several times until it reached its current site in Piura.

hechos/rescate-de-atahualpa/resumen.texto: A prisoner in Cajamarca, Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold up to the height of his raised hand, and another twice over with silver. For months, gold and silver pieces arrived from temples and palaces, including the plates of the Coricancha of Cusco, which were melted down almost entirely into bars. According to the act of smelting and division of June 1533, about 1,326,539 pesos of gold and 51,610 marks of silver were obtained, divided between the Crown, which took the quinto, and the men of Cajamarca according to their rank.

hechos/ejecucion-de-atahualpa/resumen.texto: On July 26, 1533, with the ransom already gathered, Pizarro and his captains sentenced Atahualpa to death, accused of plotting an attack with his generals. According to the chroniclers, the killing of Huáscar, ordered by Atahualpa from prison, and the fear that he, if freed, would lead the resistance also weighed on the decision. He was baptized as Francisco before dying and was executed by garrote instead of being burned at the stake. Hernando de Soto, sent to look for the supposed army, did not find it; witnesses such as Pedro Pizarro say that several conquistadors opposed the sentence, and Charles V wrote to Pizarro that the Inca's death had displeased him. The traditional date of August 29 is an error of later chronicles.

hechos/ocupacion-del-cusco/titulo.texto: March on Cusco and Spanish founding of the city

hechos/ocupacion-del-cusco/resumen.texto: After Atahualpa's death, Pizarro advanced toward Cusco with Andean allies who were enemies of Atahualpa's generals, and who according to several chronicles had killed much of Huáscar's family and supporters in Cusco, and with the young Manco Inca, who joined him along the way. At Jaquijahuana he had the general Chalcuchímac burned alive, accused of organizing the resistance, and his vanguard suffered a setback against the troops of Quisquis at Vilcaconga. They entered Cusco on November 15, 1533, where Manco was made Inca; they sacked temples and palaces, and on March 23, 1534, Pizarro founded the Spanish city over the Inca street plan.

hechos/conquista-del-norte-del-tawantins.texto: Conquest of Quito and the northern Tawantinsuyu

In 1534 Sebastián de Belalcázar marched from San Miguel de Piura toward Quito with about two hundred Spaniards and thousands of Cañari allies, enemies of the Incas because of the repressions of Huayna Cápac and Atahualpa. He won several battles, such as Teocajas, against General Rumiñahui, who according to the chroniclers abandoned and burned Quito before his arrival. Pedro de Alvarado came from Guatemala with his own force to contest the region, but at Riobamba Almagro bought his men and ships for one hundred thousand pesos; Rumiñahui was captured and executed in 1535.

hechos/fundacion-de-quito/titulo.texto: Founding of San Francisco de Quito

hechos/fundacion-de-quito/resumen.texto: In August 1534, on the plain of Riobamba, Diego de Almagro founded the city of Santiago de Quito and the villa of San Francisco de Quito, to secure the region against Pedro de Alvarado.
