On December 6, 1534, Sebastián de Belalcázar established San Francisco de Quito on the ruins of the Inca city, which had been the center of the northern Tawantinsuyu.

hechos/fundacion-de-lima/resumen.texto: On January 18, 1535, Pizarro founded the City of the Kings in the Rímac valley, on lands of the curaca Taulichusco, to have a capital near the sea instead of Jauja or Cusco. Laid out in a grid and divided into lots among the residents, it was the seat of the governorship and from 1544 of the Audiencia and the viceroyalty, and the main Spanish city in South America.

hechos/huancas-aliados-de-los-espanoles/.texto: The Huancas, allies of the Spanish

The Huanca lords of the Mantaro valley, subjugated by the Incas in the 15th century, allied with Pizarro from his arrival at Jauja in 1533 and supported him with warriors, food and carriers against Atahualpa's generals, against Manco Inca and in the civil wars. In 1558-1561 they petitioned the king, presenting the lists of everything they had handed over, read from their quipus. The alliance did not spare them the encomienda or the mita; Waldemar Espinoza Soriano used it to argue that the conquest was also a war of Andean peoples against Inca domination.

hechos/canaris-y-chachapoyas-aliados-de-.texto: Cañaris and Chachapoyas in the service of the Spanish

The Cañaris of the south of present-day Ecuador and the Chachapoyas of northeastern Peru, punished harshly by the Incas and partly deported as mitmaq, were among the most constant allies of the Spanish. The Cañaris fought with Belalcázar against Rumiñahui and, under Francisco Chilche, defended Cusco during the siege of 1536-1537; afterward they served as guards and auxiliaries in Cusco and took part in the Vilcabamba campaign of 1572. In return they obtained privileges, which they defended with probanzas throughout the colonial period.

hechos/rebelion-de-manco-inca/resumen.texto: In April 1536 Manco Inca, who had been imprisoned and extorted by Juan and Gonzalo Pizarro, left Cusco with permission from Hernando Pizarro and called together a large army: he besieged Cusco, sent another army against Lima, and wiped out several Spanish columns in the highlands that were coming to relieve the city. The Spanish resisted with their Indigenous allies, who made up most of their forces, and with reinforcements from other colonies; in 1537 Almagro, returning from Chile, broke the siege of Cusco, and Manco withdrew to Vilcabamba. It was the largest Indigenous offensive against the Spanish during the years of the conquest of Peru.

hechos/sitio-del-cusco/resumen.texto: From May 1536 a large army of Manco Inca besieged for about ten months some one hundred ninety Spaniards and their Cañari, Chachapoya and other Indigenous allies in Cusco, setting the city on fire with flaming projectiles. The Spanish took the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, where Juan Pizarro died, and held out until the Inca army partly dispersed to return to the sowing. Spanish chroniclers estimate between 100,000 and 200,000 besiegers; these are estimates by the defenders that cannot be verified.

hechos/ataque-inca-a-lima/resumen.texto: In August 1536 an army sent by Manco Inca under Quizo Yupanqui, which had destroyed several Spanish columns in the highlands, attacked Lima and was repulsed by the cavalry; Quizo died in the fighting. Decisive were the warriors sent by Contarhuacho, lady of Huaylas and mother of Quispe Sisa, companion of Francisco Pizarro, and other Indigenous allies from the coast.

hechos/batalla-de-ollantaytambo/resumen.texto: In early 1537 Hernando Pizarro attacked the fortress of Ollantaytambo, Manco Inca's base, with about seventy horsemen and thousands of Indigenous allies. The Incas repulsed them from the terraces and flooded the plain by diverting the river, in one of the few outright defeats of the Spanish in the conquest; shortly afterward Manco left the place and withdrew to the jungle of Vilcabamba.

hechos/estado-neoinca-de-vilcabamba/resu.texto: After the failure of the uprising, Manco Inca established in the mountains and jungle of Vilcabamba, northwest of Cusco, an independent kingdom with centers at Vitcos and Vilcabamba, from where his warriors attacked the road from Lima to Cusco and the towns allied with the Spanish. In 1539 an expedition led by Gonzalo Pizarro plundered the region and captured the coya Cura Ocllo, who was executed. His successors Sayri Túpac, Titu Cusi and Túpac Amaru negotiated with the Spanish governors for decades, until the conquest of 1572.

hechos/asesinato-de-manco-inca/resumen.texto: A group of Almagrists who had taken refuge in Vitcos after Chupas, and to whom Manco Inca had granted asylum, stabbed him to death while they were playing herrón, at the end of 1544 or the beginning of 1545, apparently hoping to win the viceroy's pardon. The Inca's guards killed them at once. Titu Cusi, who was a child and present, described the scene in his Instruction.

hechos/guerras-civiles-entre-conquistado.texto: Civil wars among the conquistadors of Peru

From 1537 the Spaniards of Peru fought one another: first Pizarristas and Almagristas over Cusco (Abancay, Las Salinas, the murder of Pizarro, Chupas), then the encomenderos against the Crown over the New Laws (Iñaquito, Huarina, Jaquijahuana), and finally the rebellion of Hernández Girón (1553-1554). Thousands of Indigenous people fought in all of these as auxiliaries and carriers, and both sides requisitioned food and people from the communities; Carlos Sempat Assadourian argued that these wars weighed on the fall of the Andean population more than was believed.

hechos/batalla-de-las-salinas/resumen.texto: On April 6, 1538, near Cusco, the army of Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro defeated the troops of Diego de Almagro, who had taken the city on his return from Chile, claiming that it lay within his governorship. Almagro was captured, tried and executed in July 1538 by order of Hernando Pizarro; according to the chroniclers, thousands of Indigenous people watched the battle from the hills.

hechos/asesinato-de-francisco-pizarro/re.texto: On June 26, 1541, some twenty Almagrists led by Juan de Rada entered Pizarro's house in Lima and killed him. They proclaimed as governor Diego de Almagro the Younger, son of the executed adelantado, which opened a new war against the supporters of the Crown.

hechos/batalla-de-chupas/resumen.texto: On September 16, 1542, near Huamanga, Governor Cristóbal Vaca de Castro, with the former Pizarristas, defeated Diego de Almagro the Younger in one of the bloodiest battles between Spaniards in the Americas. Almagro the Younger was beheaded in Cusco, and many of his followers were executed or fled, some of them to the court of Manco Inca in Vilcabamba.

hechos/batalla-de-inaquito/lugar.texto: Iñaquito, on the outskirts of Quito

hechos/batalla-de-inaquito/resumen.texto: On January 18, 1546, on the outskirts of Quito, Gonzalo Pizarro and the encomenderos who had rebelled against the New Laws defeated the first viceroy of Peru, Blasco Núñez Vela, who died in the fighting and was beheaded. Gonzalo became master of Peru, and some of his supporters, such as Francisco de Carvajal, proposed that he crown himself king.

hechos/batalla-de-huarina/resumen.texto: On October 20, 1547, beside Lake Titicaca, Gonzalo Pizarro, thanks above all to the arquebusiers of Francisco de Carvajal, defeated the royalist captain Diego Centeno in one of the battles with the most deaths in the civil wars. It was his last victory before La Gasca's arrival.

hechos/batalla-de-jaquijahuana/resumen.texto: On April 9, 1548, in the Jaquijahuana valley near Cusco, Gonzalo Pizarro faced the army of Pedro de la Gasca, which carried the suspension of the most contested laws and a pardon for those who switched sides; most of Pizarro's men deserted before fighting. Gonzalo Pizarro and Francisco de Carvajal were executed the next day, and La Gasca distributed the encomiendas of the rebels among the loyalists.

hechos/rebelion-de-hernandez-giron/resum.texto: In November 1553 the encomendero Francisco Hernández Girón rose up in Cusco against the Audiencia of Lima, which governed without a viceroy and enforced the prohibition of the personal service of the Indians. He raised an army with African slaves, to whom he promised freedom, and defeated the royalists at Chuquinga, but he was defeated at Pucará in October 1554 and executed in Lima. It was the last uprising of the encomenderos against the Crown.

hechos/expedicion-de-la-canela/titulo.texto: Gonzalo Pizarro's expedition to La Canela

hechos/expedicion-de-la-canela/resumen.texto: In 1541 Gonzalo Pizarro left Quito for the east in search of the “land of cinnamon” with about 220 Spaniards and some 4,000 Indigenous servants, many of them taken by force. The expedition was lost in the jungle; Francisco de Orellana split off with a brigantine and went down the Amazon to the Atlantic, and Gonzalo returned to Quito in 1542 with some eighty surviving Spaniards. According to the chroniclers, almost all the Indigenous members of the expedition died of hunger, cold and disease.

hechos/encomienda-en-el-peru/resumen.texto: From 1534 Pizarro distributed the Andean peoples in encomiendas: each encomendero collected tribute in goods and labor from the Indians in his charge, with the legal obligation to protect them and to pay for their doctrina. In the first decades there was no fixed tribute and the abuses were severe, as Domingo de Santo Tomás and the oidor Hernando de Santillán denounced; La Gasca ordered the first general tribute assessment in 1549, and the New Laws and later royal cédulas limited personal service and inheritance. From the mid-1550s the encomenderos offered the king money for perpetuity, and around 1560-1562 the curacas, with the support of Domingo de Santo Tomás and Las Casas, offered to pay more to prevent it; the Crown did not grant it, and the encomiendas gradually lapsed until their abolition in 1720.

hechos/audiencia-de-lima/titulo.texto: Creation of the Audiencia of Lima

hechos/audiencia-de-lima/resumen.texto: The New Laws of 1542 created the Royal Audiencia of Lima, a superior court and governing body with jurisdiction over almost all of Spanish South America, which was installed in 1544 with Viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela. Its oidores deposed that same viceroy that year and governed Peru during periods without a viceroy.

hechos/primer-concilio-limense/resumen.texto: A provincial council convened by Archbishop Jerónimo de Loayza with representatives of the dioceses of Peru. It ordered that the doctrine be taught to Indians with a common catechism in their language, that the huacas be destroyed, and that parish priests not charge Indians for the sacraments.

hechos/segundo-concilio-limense/resumen.texto: A second provincial council, also presided over by Loayza, which gathered the norms of evangelization after two decades: it required priests of Indian parishes to know their parishioners' language, ordered the fight against the worship of the huacas and of the mummies of ancestors, and regulated life in the doctrinas. Its decrees prepared those of the Third Council of 1582-1583.

hechos/salida-de-sayri-tupac/titulo.texto: Departure of Sayri Túpac from Vilcabamba

hechos/salida-de-sayri-tupac/resumen.texto: After years of negotiations, the Inca Sayri Túpac left Vilcabamba and arrived in Lima in January 1558, where Viceroy Andrés Hurtado de Mendoza granted him a pardon and encomiendas in the Yucay valley in exchange for his renouncing his rights. He was baptized as Diego in Cusco and died in 1561; his brothers Titu Cusi and Túpac Amaru, who remained in Vilcabamba, kept the independent kingdom.

hechos/audiencia-de-quito/titulo.texto: Creation of the Audiencia of Quito

hechos/audiencia-de-quito/resumen.texto: By royal cédula of 1563, Philip II created the Royal Audiencia of Quito, separating from the direct government of Lima a territory that covered present-day Ecuador and parts of southern Colombia and northern Peru. It was the territorial basis of republican Ecuador.

hechos/corregimientos-de-indios/resumen.texto: In 1565 Governor Lope García de Castro established the corregidores of Indians: Spanish officials in charge of each Indigenous province, to collect tribute, administer justice and protect the Indians from encomenderos and curacas. Over time they became one of the main sources of abuse: from the late 17th century they bought the post and recovered the cost through the forced distribution of goods, as Guaman Poma denounced and, in the 18th century, Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa.

hechos/capitulacion-de-acobamba/resumen.texto: Agreement of 1566 between envoys of Governor Lope García de Castro and the Inca Titu Cusi, who accepted the sovereignty of the king and the entry of missionaries and a corregidor in exchange for recognition of his lordship in Vilcabamba and revenues for himself and for his son, who would marry Beatriz, daughter of Sayri Túpac. Titu Cusi was baptized in 1568 and received Augustinian friars, but the agreement was never fully applied and it broke down in 1572.

hechos/taki-onqoy/resumen.texto: A religious movement detected in 1564 in the Huamanga region, whose preachers, such as Juan Chocne, announced that the huacas, defeated by the Christian God, would defeat him again and wipe out the Spanish, and called for rejecting everything Spanish. Their followers fell into trances while singing and dancing (“taki onqoy” means “sickness of song”). It is known above all from the service reports of the visitor Cristóbal de Albornoz, who pursued it around 1569-1571 and punished its leaders, and from the chronicle of Cristóbal de Molina. Luis Millones, Nathan Wachtel and Steve Stern interpreted it as a millenarian movement of resistance; Pedro Guibovich, Gabriela Ramos and Juan Carlos Estenssoro argued that Albornoz enlarged its reach and unity to make his own merits count.

hechos/llegada-de-los-jesuitas-al-peru/t.texto: Arrival of the Jesuits in Peru

hechos/llegada-de-los-jesuitas-al-peru/r.texto: In 1568 the first Jesuits arrived in Lima. They founded colleges in Lima, Cusco, Potosí, Arequipa, La Paz and Quito, took over the doctrina of Juli in 1576, which became a center for the study of Aymara and had a printing press, and played a central role in the Third Council, with José de Acosta, in the teaching of Indigenous languages and in the extirpation campaigns of the 17th century.

hechos/reducciones-toledanas/resumen.texto: During his general visitation, Viceroy Francisco de Toledo ordered the concentration of the Indigenous population, which lived dispersed in small settlements, into new towns laid out on the Spanish model, with a plaza, a church, an Indigenous cabildo and a jail, to facilitate the collection of tribute, the mita, evangelization and control. It was one of the largest forced resettlements of population of its time: hundreds of thousands of people left their old towns, and abandoned houses were ordered torn down to prevent their return. Over time many Indigenous people returned to their lands or fled to other provinces as forasteros, to avoid paying tribute or going to the mita, and part of the lands left empty was sold to Spaniards through land composiciones from the 1590s.

hechos/ejecucion-de-tupac-amaru-i/titulo.texto: Conquest of Vilcabamba and execution of Túpac Amaru I

hechos/ejecucion-de-tupac-amaru-i/resume.texto: After a Spanish envoy was killed on the Vilcabamba frontier, Viceroy Toledo declared war on the Inca kingdom in April 1572: an army of Spaniards and thousands of Indigenous allies, among them Cañaris, took Vilcabamba in June, and Martín García de Loyola captured Túpac Amaru in the jungle. Taken to Cusco, he was sentenced in a summary trial and beheaded in the plaza on September 24, 1572, before a crowd, despite pleas for clemency from clerics, friars and residents. Garcilaso and Guaman Poma condemned the execution; the phrase that tradition says Philip II addressed to Toledo, that he had sent him to serve kings and not to kill them, is not documented.

hechos/mina-de-huancavelica/resumen.texto: In 1563-1564 the encomendero Amador de Cabrera registered the mercury deposit of Santa Bárbara in Huancavelica, whose cinnabar the Andean peoples used as a pigment. From 1570 the Crown reserved the mercury, and Toledo assigned the mine a mita of several thousand Indigenous people from neighboring provinces, because mercury was indispensable for refining the silver of Potosí by amalgamation. The mitayos worked in galleries with mercury vapors and the risk of cave-ins, and chronic poisoning sickened and killed them; viceroys, religious figures and inspectors described it as one of the deadliest burdens of the viceroyalty. The mita of Huancavelica continued, with reforms, until its abolition by the Cortes of Cádiz.

hechos/guerra-contra-los-chiriguanos/tit.texto: Viceroy Toledo's war against the Chiriguanos

hechos/guerra-contra-los-chiriguanos/res.texto: The Chiriguanos, Guaraní-speaking peoples of the eastern cordillera of Charcas who had resisted the Incas, attacked the Spanish frontiers and held the Chanés of the lowlands in servitude. In 1574 Viceroy Toledo, after declaring war on them, personally led an expedition from La Plata that failed in the highlands because of hunger, disease and Chiriguano attacks. The Chiriguano frontier was sustained with forts and missions until the 19th century.

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-lima/resumen.texto: In 1584 the Audiencia of Lima authorized Antonio Ricardo, an Italian printer who had come from Mexico, to print in the city. His first printed work was a royal decree on the reform of the calendar, and the next was the trilingual Doctrina christiana of the Third Council, the first book printed in South America. The Lima press published mainly religious texts, grammars and vocabularies of Indigenous languages, laws and news accounts.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-santa-a.texto: Founding of the Hospital of Santa Ana in Lima
Hospital de Santa Ana de Lima

Archbishop Jerónimo de Loayza founded the hospital of Santa Ana in Lima in 1549 to serve Indigenous people, and left it his property; it was sustained by alms, rents and a contribution collected from the tribute-paying Indigenous people themselves. It was part of a network of hospitals separated by groups, with others for Spaniards (San Andrés), sailors (Espíritu Santo) and people of African origin (San Bartolomé), and in Cusco, Quito, Potosí and other cities there were hospitals for natives with similar functions.

hechos/colegios-de-caciques/titulo.texto: Colleges for the sons of caciques

hechos/colegios-de-caciques/resumen.texto: At the initiative of the Jesuits and Viceroy Esquilache, colleges were opened for the eldest sons of caciques, the future rulers of their towns: the Príncipe college in the Cercado of Lima and the San Francisco de Borja college in Cusco. They taught doctrine, reading, writing, Latin and music, with the declared purpose of making them faithful Christians and turning them away from their parents' religion, in the context of the extirpation campaigns. The Jesuits directed them until their expulsion in 1767; afterward both continued to operate under another administration.

hechos/universidades-de-quito/resumen.texto: In Quito, three institutions that granted degrees operated in the 17th century: the university of San Fulgencio of the Augustinians, authorized at the end of the 16th century; the university of San Gregorio Magno of the Jesuits, in their Colegio Máximo from 1620-1622; and the university of Santo Tomás de Aquino of the Dominicans, founded in 1688. After the expulsion of the Jesuits they were unified into the Universidad de Santo Tomás, the forerunner of the Central University of Ecuador.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-hu.texto: Founding of the University of Huamanga
Universidad de San Cristóbal de Huamanga
In 1677 the bishop of Huamanga, Cristóbal de Castilla y Zamora, founded the Universidad de San Cristóbal, later approved by the king and the pope, to train clerics and lawyers for the region.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-sa.texto: Founding of the University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco
Universidad de San Antonio Abad del Cusco

By a bull of Innocent XII in 1692, the seminary of San Antonio Abad in Cusco, where Juan de Espinosa Medrano had taught, obtained the right to confer university degrees. In Cusco the Jesuit university of San Ignacio de Loyola had already been granting degrees since 1621; it disappeared with the expulsion of 1767.

hechos/escuela-cusquena/resumen.texto: A tradition of religious painting in Cusco that began with European masters such as Bernardo Bitti and was developed by Indigenous and mestizo painters such as Diego Quispe Tito and Basilio de Santa Cruz Pumacallao. In 1688 the Indigenous painters separated from the guild they had shared with Spaniards. In the 18th century the workshops produced thousands of paintings in series for the whole viceroyalty, with Virgins in triangular mantles, gilded brocades, archangels with arquebuses, and landscapes with Andean flora and fauna.

hechos/escuela-quitena/resumen.texto: A tradition of religious painting and sculpture in Quito, born in the school of arts and trades for Indigenous people that the Franciscans opened around 1550 in the convent of San Francisco. Its workshops, with Indigenous, mestizo and Creole artists such as Miguel de Santiago, Bernardo de Legarda and Manuel Chili “Caspicara,” sent carved and polychrome wooden images and paintings to much of Spanish America in the 17th and 18th centuries.

hechos/obrajes-de-quito/titulo.texto: The obrajes of the Audiencia of Quito

hechos/obrajes-de-quito/resumen.texto: In the highlands of the Audiencia of Quito, obrajes multiplied from the late 16th century: textile workshops producing wool and cotton cloth, run by communities, encomenderos, private individuals and religious orders, which sold cloth to Lima, Potosí and New Granada. Indigenous people worked in them through the mita, debt or criminal sentence, under long hours and confinement that officials denounced from the 16th century and that Juan and Ulloa denounced in the 18th. Competition from European textiles sank the activity in the late 18th century.

hechos/rebelion-de-las-alcabalas/titulo.texto: Rebellion over the alcabalas in Quito

hechos/rebelion-de-las-alcabalas/resumen.texto: In 1592 the cabildo and residents of Quito resisted the application of the alcabala, the sales tax that Philip II extended to the viceroyalty, and the protest turned into a riot against the Audiencia. The viceroy sent troops that entered the city in 1593, and several ringleaders were executed.

hechos/zambos-de-esmeraldas/resumen.texto: From the mid-16th century, Africans who arrived through shipwrecks or fled, such as the group of Alonso de Illescas (1553) and another led by the family of Francisco de Arobe, son of an African man and an Indigenous woman, joined Indigenous peoples of the Esmeraldas coast and formed independent communities of mixed population, which the Spanish called “zambos.” After several military and missionary expeditions failed, the Audiencia of Quito negotiated their incorporation: in 1599 the Indigenous painter Andrés Sánchez Gallque portrayed Don Francisco de Arobe and his sons, dressed in the Spanish manner and adorned with Indigenous gold, to send the painting to the king as proof of the “pacification.”

hechos/esclavitud-africana-en-el-peru/re.texto: Enslaved Africans arrived in Peru with the conquistadors; the Capitulation of Toledo had already authorized Pizarro to bring them. In the following decades many more arrived through Cartagena and Panama to work as servants, artisans, field laborers on haciendas and coastal vineyards, and muleteers; in the first half of the 17th century the Black and mulatto population, enslaved and free, was close to half that of Lima. Many gained their freedom through purchase or manumission and formed cofradías; slavery was abolished in Peru in 1854.

hechos/extirpacion-de-idolatrias/resumen.texto: From 1609, following the denunciations of the priest Francisco de Ávila in Huarochirí, the archdiocese of Lima organized visits to uncover and punish Andean cults that were still alive. The visitors, accompanied by Jesuits such as Arriaga, questioned communities, burned the mummies of ancestors (mallquis) and cult objects, destroyed huacas, and punished Andean religious specialists with lashes, shearing of hair or confinement. There were intense campaigns under Archbishops Lobo Guerrero (1609-1622) and Villagómez (1641-1671), and isolated cases until the 18th century; Kenneth Mills showed from the case files that Andean religion mixed with Christianity rather than disappearing.

hechos/epidemias-andinas-del-siglo-xvi/t.texto: Epidemics in the Andes in the 16th century

hechos/epidemias-andinas-del-siglo-xvi/r.texto: Apart from the epidemic before the arrival of the Spanish in which, according to the chroniclers, Huayna Cápac died (perhaps of smallpox, although this is debated), the Andes suffered new epidemics recorded by chroniclers and authorities: one in 1546, perhaps typhus or plague; the smallpox and measles epidemic of 1558-1560; and the great epidemic of 1585-1591, of smallpox, measles and typhus, which spread from Cartagena and Quito to Charcas and Chile. According to Noble David Cook, these were the main cause of the fall of the Andean population, aggravated by war, forced labor and social disorganization.

hechos/caida-de-la-poblacion-andina/titu.texto: Decline of the Indigenous population of the central Andes

hechos/caida-de-la-poblacion-andina/resu.texto: The population of Peru fell catastrophically in the century after the conquest. Estimates for 1520 range from about two million (Ángel Rosenblat) to more than thirty million (Henry Dobyns), depending on the author and method; Noble David Cook proposed about nine million and some 600,000 around 1620, and the visitas and censuses of the 16th century, such as Toledo's general count of the 1570s, make it possible to follow the decline with more reliable figures. Most historians attribute the fall mainly to epidemics, aggravated by wars, forced relocations, labor in mines and obrajes, and the disorganization of production; on the coast the Indigenous population almost disappeared.

hechos/terremoto-de-lima-de-1746/titulo.texto: Earthquake and tsunami of Lima and Callao

hechos/terremoto-de-lima-de-1746/resumen.texto: On the night of October 28, 1746, an earthquake destroyed much of Lima, and shortly afterward a tsunami swept through the port of Callao, from which very few of its inhabitants survived. In Lima more than a thousand people died, according to contemporary estimates. Viceroy Manso de Velasco directed the reconstruction and built the Real Felipe fortress; according to Charles Walker, his attempts to reform the city clashed with the Church and the elites, and fear of an Indigenous rebellion contributed to the harsh repression of the conspiracy of 1750.

hechos/reparto-de-mercancias/resumen.texto: The corregidores of Indians, who purchased their posts, obliged communities to buy mules, clothing, iron and other goods from them at prices they set, and collected by force. Forbidden by law, it was legalized and given set rates between 1751 and 1756 to limit it, but the abuses continued; Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa denounced it, and Scarlett O'Phelan linked it to the wave of revolts of the 18th century. The intendant system of 1784 abolished it, after the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II.

hechos/rebelion-de-juan-santos-atahualpa.texto: In May 1742 Juan Santos Atahualpa, who presented himself as a descendant of Atahualpa and the legitimate Inca, raised the Asháninka, Yanesha, Piro and other peoples of the central jungle of Peru, where the Franciscans had founded missions and colonist towns since the beginning of the century. The rebels destroyed the missions and defeated the viceregal expeditions of 1742-1746, and in 1752 they occupied the highland town of Andamarca for several days. The viceroy chose to close the frontier with forts, and the region remained outside Spanish control until the 19th century; according to the statements recorded by the missionaries, Juan Santos announced a new order without Spaniards or Black people, although he called himself a Christian.

hechos/mision-geodesica-francesa/titulo.texto: French geodesic mission to the Audiencia of Quito

hechos/mision-geodesica-francesa/resumen.texto: An expedition of the Paris Academy of Sciences, with permission from the Spanish Crown, to measure an arc of meridian near the equator and test whether the Earth was flattened at the poles, as Newton held. It included Louis Godin, Pierre Bouguer and Charles-Marie de La Condamine, along with the Spanish naval officers Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa and the collaboration of Pedro Vicente Maldonado, a native of Quito, and it worked in the Andes of Quito between 1736 and 1744. Its measurements confirmed the flattening, and its members gave the first European scientific descriptions of the cinchona tree, rubber and platinum.

hechos/misiones-de-maynas/resumen.texto: From 1638 the Jesuits of Quito founded, from the city of San Francisco de Borja, some sixty missions among the Maynas, Jeberos, Omaguas, Cocamas and other peoples of the upper Amazon and the Marañón. Smallpox and measles epidemics repeatedly decimated the resettled populations, and attacks by Portuguese slave raiders and Indigenous rebellions destroyed several missions. Samuel Fritz defended the frontier against Portugal and drew his map of the Amazon; after the expulsion of the Jesuits the missions passed to the Franciscans and declined.

hechos/misiones-de-moxos-y-chiquitos/tit.texto: Jesuit missions of Moxos and Chiquitos

hechos/misiones-de-moxos-y-chiquitos/res.texto: From the founding of Loreto in 1682, the Jesuits of the Province of Peru established in the Moxos plains about twenty missions with peoples speaking Moxo, Baure and other languages, and from 1691 those of the Province of Paraguay founded ten more in Chiquitos. Organized like those of Paraguay, they had Indigenous cabildos, cattle raising, weaving workshops, silverwork and instrument making, and an intense musical life, and they served as a frontier against the Portuguese; epidemics caused heavy losses. After the expulsion of 1767 they passed to parish priests and civil administrators and declined; the churches of Chiquitos are World Heritage Sites.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas-del-per.texto: Expulsion of the Jesuits from Peru and Quito

In 1767 Viceroy Manuel de Amat in Peru and the president of the Audiencia in Quito carried out Charles III's order to expel the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits, among them Juan Pablo Viscardo, were shipped to Europe, and their colleges, haciendas, missions and printing presses passed to the administration of the Temporalidades. The expulsion left the reductions of Maynas, Moxos and Chiquitos without missionaries and closed their colleges and universities in Cusco (San Ignacio de Loyola) and Quito (San Gregorio Magno).

hechos/rebelion-de-los-barrios-de-quito/.texto: Revolt of the neighborhoods of Quito

In May 1765 the popular neighborhoods of Quito, with mestizos, Indigenous people and poor Creoles, rose up against the aguardiente monopoly and the new administration of the alcabala, attacked the monopoly house, and for months controlled the city and demanded the departure of the peninsulares. The Audiencia had to suspend the reforms and grant a pardon, and in 1766 troops sent from outside restored control.

hechos/conspiracion-de-lima-y-huarochiri.texto: Conspiracy of Lima and rebellion of Huarochirí

In 1750 the authorities uncovered in Lima a conspiracy of Indigenous people and mestizos to take the city, and several of the conspirators were executed. One of them, Francisco Jiménez Inca, fled to Huarochirí and raised several towns of the province; the rebellion was suppressed within a few weeks and its leaders executed.

hechos/expedicion-botanica-al-peru/titul.texto: Botanical expedition to Peru and Chile

hechos/expedicion-botanica-al-peru/resum.texto: An expedition sent by Charles III with the botanists Hipólito Ruiz and José Pavón and the French physician Joseph Dombey to study the flora of Peru and Chile, especially useful plants such as cinchona. It traveled the coast, the highlands, the Peruvian ceja de selva and central Chile, with artists who painted hundreds of plates, and sent seeds, living plants and herbaria to Madrid.

hechos/revolucion-de-quito-de-1809/resum.texto: On August 10, 1809, a group of Creoles from Quito deposed the president of the Audiencia, Count Ruiz de Castilla, and formed a Sovereign Junta presided over by the Marquis of Selva Alegre, which would govern in the name of Ferdinand VII for as long as the French occupation of Spain lasted. The other provinces of the Audiencia did not follow, the viceroy of Peru sent troops, and the junta dissolved in October; in Ecuador the date is remembered as the “first cry of independence.”

hechos/matanza-del-2-de-agosto-de-1810/r.texto: The leaders of the 1809 junta were imprisoned and tried. On August 2, 1810, during a popular attempt to free them, royalist troops who had come from Lima killed most of the prisoners in the barracks and then some three hundred people in the city, according to later estimates. The massacre led to the formation of a new junta in Quito.

hechos/estado-de-quito/resumen.texto: The second junta of Quito, formed in September 1810 with the royal commissioner Carlos Montúfar, refused to recognize the Regency Council, and in 1812 a congress proclaimed the State of Quito with its own constitution. Facing Cuenca and Guayaquil, which remained loyal to the Regency, and troops sent from Lima, it was defeated at the end of 1812.

hechos/rebelion-del-cusco-de-1814/resume.texto: In August 1814 the Angulo brothers, Creoles of Cusco, with the support of the cacique Mateo Pumacahua, seized control of the city invoking the Constitution of Cádiz and sent expeditions to Arequipa, La Paz and Huamanga, with broad Indigenous participation. It was the broadest movement in Peru before San Martín's arrival; the troops of Viceroy Abascal defeated it at Umachiri in March 1815, and its leaders were executed, among them Pumacahua and the poet Mariano Melgar.

hechos/independencia-de-guayaquil/resume.texto: On October 9, 1820, Creoles and officers of Guayaquil deposed the royalist authorities and proclaimed the Free Province of Guayaquil, with the poet José Joaquín de Olmedo as its head. It appealed for help to Bolívar and San Martín and became the base for Sucre's campaign against Quito; in 1822 Bolívar incorporated it into Gran Colombia.

hechos/batalla-de-pichincha/resumen.texto: On May 24, 1822, on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano above Quito, the army of Antonio José de Sucre, with Colombian troops and a division sent by San Martín from Peru, defeated the royalists of General Melchor Aymerich. The capitulation handed over Quito and the territory of the former Audiencia, which joined Gran Colombia.

hechos/independencia-de-bolivia/resumen.texto: After Ayacucho, Sucre occupied Upper Peru, where the last royalist leader, Pedro Antonio de Olañeta, died at Tumusla in April 1825. An assembly of deputies from the Upper Peruvian provinces, meeting in Chuquisaca, declared on August 6, 1825, the independence of a new state, which it called República Bolívar and then Bolivia, rather than join Peru or the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. The war had begun in 1809, with the juntas of Chuquisaca and La Paz, the republiquetas and the expeditions sent from Buenos Aires.

hechos/mito-de-los-ocho-millones-de-muer.texto: The figure of eight million dead in Potosí

A widely repeated figure holds that the Cerro Rico of Potosí cost eight million Indigenous lives over three centuries. It was spread by Eduardo Galeano in Open Veins of Latin America (1971), which attributes it to a nineteenth-century author, and it does not come from any record of the period. The documents of the mita show that Toledo fixed a contingent of about thirteen to fourteen thousand mitayos per year, who worked in rotations, and that it later declined: even adding up all those sent between 1573 and 1812 does not reach half that figure, and Noble David Cook estimates the Indigenous population of all of Peru around 1620 at about 600,000 people. No study of the mita, such as those of Peter Bakewell and Jeffrey Cole, supports a number of that order. Those same studies document, on the other hand, high mortality from accidents, lung diseases and mercury poisoning, and the mass flight of communities to escape the service.

hechos/mito-del-tesoro-de-los-llanganate.texto: The legend of the Llanganates treasure

According to a legend, General Rumiñahui hid in the Llanganates mountains, in present-day Ecuador, the gold that was being taken to Cajamarca for Atahualpa's ransom. It rests on an alleged route written by a Spaniard named Valverde, which the botanist Richard Spruce made known in 1860-1861, and it has since inspired numerous expeditions; there is no document from the time of the conquest that supports it, and no search has found the treasure.

hechos/independencia-del-ecuador/titulo.texto: Separation of Ecuador from Gran Colombia

hechos/independencia-del-ecuador/resumen.texto: In May 1830 an assembly of Quito notables decided to separate the former Southern District from Gran Colombia and to constitute an independent state, Ecuador, with the Venezuelan general Juan José Flores as its head. It completed a process that had begun with the junta of 1809 and continued with the independence of Guayaquil (1820) and the battle of Pichincha (1822).

lugares/cajamarca/resumen.texto: City in the northern highlands of Peru, an Inca provincial center with a plaza, palaces, hot baths and a temple of the Sun, where Atahualpa was resting with his army when Pizarro arrived. He was captured in its plaza on November 16, 1532, and executed there in 1533. It later became the seat of a colonial corregimiento with obrajes and a large Indigenous population.

lugares/cuarto-del-rescate/resumen.texto: Inca stone building in the center of Cajamarca, the only Inca construction still standing in the city. Tradition identifies it with the room that Atahualpa offered to fill with gold in exchange for his freedom, or with the place where he was held prisoner; contemporary testimony does not allow this to be verified.

lugares/vitcos/resumen.texto: Inca palace on a hilltop in the Vilcabamba valley, the first residence of Manco Inca after his withdrawal in 1537 and where he was murdered in 1544. Nearby is the sacred rock of Chuquipalta or Ñusta Hispana, whose sanctuary the Augustinian friars burned around 1570. Hiram Bingham identified it in 1911.

lugares/vilcabamba/resumen.texto: Ruins in the high jungle of Cusco, at Espíritu Pampa, of the last capital of the independent Inca state, which its inhabitants set on fire and abandoned before the troops of Viceroy Toledo entered in June 1572. Hiram Bingham passed the site in 1911 without recognizing it; Gene Savoy identified it in 1964, and the Spanish-style roof tiles found there match the descriptions in the chronicles.

lugares/san-miguel-de-piura/resumen.texto: The first city founded by the Spanish in present-day Peru, in 1532, under the name San Miguel, in the Tangarará valley; it was moved several times until it reached its current site. It was the base from which Pizarro marched to Cajamarca and Belalcázar to Quito.

lugares/quito/resumen.texto: Andean city in present-day Ecuador, center of the northern Tawantinsuyu in the time of Huayna Cápac and Atahualpa, founded as a Spanish city in 1534 over the ruins of the Inca city. It has been the seat of the Audiencia of Quito since 1563, with a bishopric, universities, convents and the workshops of the Quito school, and it is the capital of Ecuador. Its historic center was among the first sites declared World Heritage Sites, in 1978.

lugares/huancavelica/resumen.texto: City in the central highlands of Peru, founded in 1571 by order of Viceroy Toledo as Villa Rica de Oropesa, beside the Santa Bárbara mercury mine, the largest in the Americas. The mercury from its mine was indispensable for amalgamating Potosí’s silver, and its forced mita was one of the most feared in the viceroyalty.

lugares/trujillo-peru/resumen.texto: City on the north coast of Peru founded by Diego de Almagro at the end of 1534 and confirmed by Pizarro in 1535, near the ruins of Chan Chan, the Chimú capital. It was the seat of a bishopric and the center of a region of sugar haciendas worked by Indigenous and African enslaved labor.

lugares/arequipa/resumen.texto: City in southern Peru founded in 1540 as Villa Hermosa de Arequipa, with buildings of white volcanic sillar stone. It was a center of encomenderos and vineyards, suffered earthquakes and the great eruption of the Huaynaputina volcano in 1600, and its Santa Catalina monastery, founded in 1579, is one of the best-preserved colonial complexes in the Americas.

lugares/huamanga/resumen.texto: City in the central highlands of Peru founded in 1539 as San Juan de la Frontera de Huamanga to protect the road from Lima to Cusco from attacks by Manco Inca. It was a center of encomiendas, a bishopric from 1609, and the seat of a university from 1677; the Taki Onqoy arose in its region. Nearby, the battle of Ayacucho was fought in 1824, from which it took its current name.

lugares/guayaquil/resumen.texto: Pacific port founded and moved several times between 1534 and 1547 to its present site beside the Guayas River. It was the main shipyard on the South American Pacific coast and the port of cacao, which made it grow in the 18th century; on October 9, 1820, it proclaimed its independence.

lugares/cuenca-ecuador/resumen.texto: City in the southern highlands of present-day Ecuador founded in 1557 by Gil Ramírez Dávalos, by order of Viceroy Andrés Hurtado de Mendoza, beside the ruins of Tomebamba, the Inca city built in Cañari territory. Its historic center is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/la-paz/resumen.texto: City founded in 1548 by Alonso de Mendoza, by order of La Gasca, as Nuestra Señora de La Paz, in memory of the end of Gonzalo Pizarro’s rebellion and to secure the road between Cusco and Potosí. A commercial city in Aymara territory, it was besieged by Túpac Katari in 1781, formed the Junta Tuitiva in 1809, and is the seat of the government of Bolivia.

lugares/callao/resumen.texto: Port of Lima and the main Pacific port of the viceroyalty of Peru, through which the silver of Potosí was shipped to Panama and Spain. English corsairs and a Dutch squadron attacked it in 1624, and the tsunami of 1746 razed it, after which the Real Felipe fortress was built.

lugares/fortaleza-del-real-felipe/resume.texto: Fortress of Callao built between 1747 and 1774 by order of Viceroy Manso de Velasco, after the 1746 tsunami destroyed the port and its defenses. It was the last royalist stronghold in Peru: General José Ramón Rodil defended it until January 1826.

lugares/hospital-de-santa-ana/nombre.texto: Hospital de Santa Ana de Lima

lugares/hospital-de-santa-ana/resumen.texto: Hospital for Indigenous people founded in Lima in 1549 by Archbishop Jerónimo de Loayza, which treated the Indians of the city and its surroundings and poor women. In the 20th century the institution was moved and continues as the Hospital Nacional Arzobispo Loayza.

lugares/universidad-de-san-antonio-abad/.texto: Universidad de San Antonio Abad del Cusco

University of Cusco that grew out of the seminary of San Antonio Abad, which obtained in 1692 the right to confer degrees by a bull of Innocent XII. It trained clergy and lawyers from the southern Andes and still operates as a national university.

lugares/universidad-de-huamanga/nombre.texto: Universidad de San Cristóbal de Huamanga

lugares/universidad-de-huamanga/resumen.texto: University founded in 1677 by Bishop Cristóbal de Castilla y Zamora in Huamanga to train clergy and letrados of the region. It was closed from the late 19th century and reopened in 1959.

lugares/colegio-de-san-borja/nombre.texto: College of San Francisco de Borja of Cusco

lugares/colegio-de-san-borja/resumen.texto: College founded in Cusco in 1621 under Viceroy Esquilache and run by the Jesuits, to educate the eldest sons of caciques in the Spanish faith and culture and to separate them from the religion of their fathers. Many caciques from the southern Andes passed through it; it continued to operate after the expulsion of the Jesuits.

lugares/iglesia-de-la-compania-quito/nom.texto: Church of La Compañía de Quito

lugares/iglesia-de-la-compania-quito/res.texto: Jesuit church in Quito built between 1605 and 1765, with a carved stone façade and an interior covered in carved and gilded wood, a major work of Quito’s Baroque. Alongside it operated the Jesuits’ Colegio Máximo, the University of San Gregorio Magno, and the procurator’s office for the Maynas missions.

lugares/convento-de-san-francisco-quito/.texto: Church and Convent of San Francisco de Quito

One of the first great religious complexes in Spanish South America, begun by the Franciscans shortly after the founding of the Spanish city. From the mid-16th century it housed a school of arts and crafts for Indigenous people and mestizos, the origin of the Quito school.

lugares/santa-rosa-de-ocopa/nombre.texto: Convent of Santa Rosa de Ocopa

lugares/santa-rosa-de-ocopa/resumen.texto: Franciscan convent founded in 1725 near Concepción, in the Mantaro valley, as the base for the missions of the central Peruvian jungle. It was a college for missionaries from 1758; from there departed the missions of Cerro de la Sal, destroyed by the rebellion of Juan Santos Atahualpa, and later those of the Ucayali.

lugares/misiones-de-chiquitos/resumen.texto: Mission towns founded by the Jesuits between 1691 and 1760 in Chiquitania, in eastern Bolivia, including San Javier, Concepción, San Rafael, San José, San Miguel, and Santa Ana. Their wooden and adobe churches, several built by Martin Schmid with Chiquitano workers, are still in use, and six of the towns were declared World Heritage Sites in 1990.

lugares/catedral-del-cusco/resumen.texto: Cathedral built between 1559 and 1654 on an Inca palace, partly with stones brought from Sacsayhuamán. It holds one of the largest collections of paintings of the Cusco school, with works by Diego Quispe Tito and Marcos Zapata, among them a Last Supper with a guinea pig on the table.

lugares/santuario-de-copacabana/resumen.texto: Shrine on the shore of Lake Titicaca, near the Island of the Sun, one of the pilgrimage centers of Inca worship. In 1583 the image of the Virgin of Candelaria, carved by the Indigenous sculptor Francisco Tito Yupanqui, a descendant of the Incas, was enthroned there; shortly afterward the shrine passed to the Augustinians and became the most important Marian center in the Andes, with a basilica built in the 17th century.
